title: A Finite Element Study of Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing of Aluminum Alloy
process_methodology: Sequentially coupled thermo-mechanical FEM (ABAQUS 2019); DFLUX subroutine for Goldak double-ellipsoid moving heat source; DC3D8 thermal and C3D8 mechanical elements.
key_params: Substrate: 260×260×25 mm; Deposition: 120×120×6 mm (2 layers); 17,687 elements; Travel speeds: 50, 100, 150, 200 mm/min; Goldak semi-axes: af=2 mm, ar=3.5 mm, b=2.2 mm, c=3 mm; Heat fractions: ff=0.4, fr=1.6.
observations:
• Evaluated four distinct deposition scan patterns: alternate line, raster line, in-out spiral, and out-in spiral.
• Out-in spiral pattern continuously concentrates thermal energy toward the component geometric center.
• Line-type scanning strategies (alternate vs. raster) exhibit nearly identical thermal histories due to negligible inter-pass interval decay.
• Increasing travel speed from 50 to 200 mm/min sharply compresses the thermal tail and reduces melt pool dwell time above solidus.
• Compressive plastic strains dominate during localized heating, transforming into severe tensile residual stresses upon final cooling.
• The maximum von Mises stress consistently concentrates at the interface between the substrate and the deposited first layer.
results:
• Thermal contours demonstrate severe heat confinement in contour/spiral modes causing asymmetric plastic warpage.
• High travel speeds yield narrower heat-affected zones and steeper temperature gradients at the trailing edge.
• Out-in spiral generates the highest peak residual stress of 244 MPa compared to 183 MPa for in-out spiral (33.3% lower).
• Peak temperature at 50 mm/min travel speed reaches 883°C, whereas at 200 mm/min it drops to 662°C.
• Simulated temperature history matched experimental thermocouple data within 5% absolute deviation.
future_work:
• Incorporating solid-state precipitate dissolution and reprecipitation kinetics (β'' phase in 6xxx Al) into the mechanical constitutive model.
• Expanding from a 2-layer simplified block to multi-layer (>20 layers) thin-wall structures to capture long-term thermal saturation.
my_comments:
• Deposition strategy dictates residual stress state even in high thermal conductivity materials like Al.
• Goldak parameters calibrated here provide an excellent initial baseline for 6xxx aluminum thermal modeling.

title: Analysis of Process Parameters, Deposition Strategies and Build Orientations in Wire-Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM)
process_methodology: Robotic GMAW-WAAM (Yaskawa Motoman HP20 + Selco Genesis 352 GSM); Central Composite Design Response Surface Methodology (CCD-RSM); 2^k Factorial Design; Vickers microhardness (HV1).
key_params: Wire diameter: 1.2 mm; Current: 80–200 A; Travel speed: 7–20 mm/s; Shielding: Ar+20% CO2 at 18 L/min; Walls: 10 & 20 layers (150 A, 11 mm/s); Cubes: 120/160 A, TS 8/15 mm/s, Hatch 2/3 mm.
observations:
• Current is the primary determinant of bead width and height, whereas travel speed predominantly controls hardness via cooling rate modulation.
• Unidirectional deposition induces pronounced cumulative height slope and wall end-slumping due to directional arc ignition dynamics.
• Bidirectional deposition completely neutralizes wall end-slumping, producing uniform vertical wall height.
• Introducing a calibrated dwell time at the end of each pass can mitigate unidirectional slumping if heat dissipation is precisely balanced.
• A microstructural transition from fine equiaxed grains at the substrate to coarse columnar dendrites occurs consistently around the 5th deposited layer.
• Thermal accumulation in tall builds (20 layers vs 10 layers) slightly lowers average hardness due to intrinsic in-situ tempering.
results:
• Microstructure transitions from fine grain boundary ferrite + pearlite near substrate to columnar Widmanstätten + acicular ferrite in upper layers.
• 90° layer-rotation strategy in cubic blocks yields uniform cross-sectional density without inter-track lack of fusion.
• Empirical RSM regression: Height = 0.713 + 0.01273·I - 0.0468·TS (R² = 89.5%); Hardness = 297.3 - 0.471·I + 4.384·TS (R² = 86.0%).
• 10-layer wall microhardness averaged 166 HV (154 bottom to 175 top); 20-layer wall averaged 156 HV (149 bottom to 171 top).
• Rapid cooling at 80 A / 20 mm/s produced peak microhardness exceeding 360 HV.
future_work:
• Dynamic closed-loop adjustment of wire feed speed and dwell time based on in-situ pyrometer temperature feedback.
• Uniaxial tensile testing and Charpy impact testing across build orientations to correlate with the observed 10 vs 20-layer grain coarsening.
my_comments:
• Layer stacking effect (10 vs 20 layers) is rarely quantified in low-carbon steel literature.
• RSM regression equations provide a fast first-order parameter selection tool for steel WAAM.

title: Effect of Double-Wire Cold Feeding on Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing of SS309L Layer Geometry
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
process_methodology: Double-wire WAAM (Primary GMAW arc wire + non-energized auxiliary cold wire feed); Taguchi L16 orthogonal array; Grey Relational Analysis (GRA); Optical microscopy and SEM-EDS.
key_params: Primary arc current: 140–200 A; Travel speed: 200–400 mm/min; Primary WFS: 4.5–7.5 m/min; Cold wire WFS: 1.5–3.5 m/min; Cold wire angle: 30–60°; Cold wire distance: 1–3 mm; Substrate: SS304 plate.
observations:
• Auxiliary cold wire absorbs sensible and latent heat of melting directly from the superheated arc column.
• Melting of non-energized filler wire reduces the net effective heat input delivered to the underlying substrate.
• Cold wire entry angle of 45° directed into the leading edge of the molten pool provides maximum arc stability without stubbing.
• Feeding cold wire too close to the arc center (<1 mm) causes arc deflection, while feeding too far (>3 mm) results in incomplete melting.
• Accelerated cooling from cold wire addition suppresses secondary dendrite arm coarsening in the austenitic matrix.
• Delta-ferrite morphology shifts from coarse vermicular to fine skeletal networks due to restricted solid-state diffusion time.
results:
• Smooth, ripple-free bead surfaces with reduced thermal spatter and improved side-wall wetting angles.
• Inter-dendritic Cr-Mo segregation is noticeably reduced due to rapid solidification kinetics.
• Deposition rate increased by 55.1% (from 1.85 kg/h for single wire to 2.87 kg/h with cold wire).
• Substrate dilution dropped from 38.4% down to 22.1%.
• Delta-ferrite volume fraction increased from 6.2 FN to 8.9 FN due to fast cooling through the delta-gamma transformation zone.
future_work:
• Multi-pass, multi-layer bulk block fabrication to evaluate inter-layer bonding integrity under high cold-wire feed rates.
• Electrochemical pitting and intergranular corrosion testing of cold-wire assisted SS309L deposits in aggressive chloride media.
my_comments:
• Auxiliary cold wire feeding decouples deposition rate from heat input—vital for distortion-sensitive structures.
• Need to consider how the altered cooling rate changes the primary solidification mode from AF to FA.

title: Parametric Study and Metallurgical Investigation of AISI 308LSi Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing Single Beads
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology, 10.1007/s00170-026-19167-2
process_methodology: GMAW-based WAAM; Full factorial single-bead experimental design; Response Surface Methodology (RSM); Schaeffler and WRC-1992 constitutional diagrams; XRD phase identification; EBSD orientation mapping.
key_params: Wire diameter: 1.0 mm (0.85 wt% Si); WFS: 3.0–7.0 m/min; TS: 0.25–0.65 m/min; Voltage: 16–22 V; Heat input: 0.28–0.78 kJ/mm; Gas: Ar+2% CO2; CTWD: 12 mm.
observations:
• High silicon content (0.85 wt% Si) reduces liquid metal surface tension, significantly enhancing melt pool spread and wetting.
• Bead contact wetting angle decreases by 18–25% compared to standard low-silicon 308L alloy wires.
• Solidification follows the Primary Ferrite (FA) mode, where delta-ferrite solidifies first and transforms partially to austenite upon cooling.
• Low heat input preserves fine vermicular and lathy delta-ferrite networks, while high heat input promotes ferrite dissolution.
• Silicon promotes strong deoxidation during droplet transfer, completely eliminating gas pore formation in single beads.
• Increasing travel speed at constant wire feed speed leads to humping and bead discontinuity beyond 0.55 m/min.
results:
• Flatter bead crown geometry with smooth transition to substrate, ideal for multi-bead overlap without valley defects.
• EBSD shows cellular dendritic morphology with strong <001> fiber texture aligned normal to the fusion boundary.
• Optimal parameter window established at WFS = 4.5–5.5 m/min and TS = 0.35–0.45 m/min (Heat input = 0.38–0.48 kJ/mm).
• Bead aspect ratio (Width/Height) maintained between 2.2 and 3.1.
• Measured Ferrite Number (FN) ranged between 7.5 and 11.2, with microhardness averaging 195–215 HV0.5.
future_work:
• Multi-layer overlapping wall experiments to validate the optimal 66.7% flat-top overlap model (FOM) using high-silicon wire.
• High-temperature oxidation resistance testing of WAAM 308LSi components up to 800°C.
my_comments:
• Silicon addition is an effective chemical solution for improving wetting without changing mechanical arc parameters.
• Single bead morphology data is essential for setting up accurate Goldak heat source dimensions.

title: Wire and Arc Additive Manufacturing of 308L Stainless Steel Components: Optimization of Processing Parameters and Material Properties
process_methodology: Cold Metal Transfer (CMT-WAAM, Fronius TPS 4000 CMT); Multi-Objective Genetic Algorithm (MOGA) coupled with Artificial Neural Network (ANN); EBSD, TEM, XRD; Directional tensile testing.
key_params: Current: 100–180 A; Travel speed: 0.3–0.6 m/min; Interpass temperatures: 100°C, 150°C, 200°C; CMT advanced mode; Shielding: 98% Ar + 2% O2; 20-layer walls; SS304 substrate.
observations:
• CMT arc mode dramatically reduces thermal spatter and narrows the thermal influence zone compared to standard pulsed GMAW.
• Interpass temperature of 100°C maximizes cooling rate, suppressing secondary dendrite arm coarsening and preserving high dislocation density.
• Higher interpass temperatures (200°C) extend the solid-state transformation dwell time, promoting delta-ferrite dissolution into austenite.
• Microstructure displays hierarchical zoning: fine equiaxed grains near substrate, coarse columnar dendrites in the middle, and fine lathy ferrite at top.
• Anisotropic mechanical performance arises from epitaxial columnar grain growth along the vertical build direction.
• Horizontal tensile specimens exhibit higher yield strength due to grain boundary barrier strengthening transverse to loading.
results:
• Interpass temperature of 100°C yields dense vermicular delta-ferrite networks that resist microvoid coalescence.
• Fractography reveals ductile dimple rupture across all orientations with dimple size scaling with interpass temperature.
• At 100°C interpass: Horizontal YS = 365±12 MPa, UTS = 585±18 MPa, Elongation = 44±3%; Vertical YS = 338±15 MPa, UTS = 552±20 MPa, Elongation = 51±4%.
• Delta-ferrite content varied from 6.8 to 8.4 vol%.
• MOGA-ANN optimized heat input identified at 0.32 kJ/mm (Current: 125 A, TS: 0.45 m/min).
future_work:
• Post-weld solution heat treatment (1050°C water quench) to eliminate mechanical anisotropy and homogenize delta-ferrite.
• Low-cycle fatigue and fatigue crack growth rate testing under horizontal and vertical loading orientations.
my_comments:
• Clear experimental evidence of how interpass temperature directly governs tensile anisotropy in austenitic steels.
• Useful reference for calibrating thermal-microstructure coupling models in stainless steel.

title: Integrated Approach to Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) Optimization: Harnessing the Synergy of Process Parameters and Deposition Strategies
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology, 30:2478–2499
material: Multi-Alloy Systems (Ti-6Al-4V, Al alloys, Inconel 718/625, Austenitic & Duplex Steels)
process_methodology: Systematic critical review; Multiphysics synthesis across GMAW, GTAW, PAW, CMT, TOP-TIG; Deposition path planning taxonomy; Active cooling and hybrid intervention analysis.
key_params: Heat input windows (0.1–2.5 kJ/mm); Interpass temperature thresholds (50–350°C); Deposition rates (1–10 kg/h); Path types: raster, zigzag, contour, medial axis, continuous space-filling.
observations:
• Process parameter optimization alone cannot prevent geometric humping and residual stress accumulation without coordinated path planning.
• Continuous closed-loop path strategies eliminate frequent arc starts and stops, which are the primary sources of localized porosity and height irregularities.
• Progressive heat accumulation over successive layers degrades geometric accuracy and promotes coarse columnar grain growth.
• Active thermal management (thermoelectric cooling, trailing shielding gas, water-cooled baseplates) restores steep temperature gradients.
• Hybrid WAAM approaches (in-situ rolling, interpass peening, ultrasonic vibration) shatter epitaxial columnar grains, promoting CET.
• Interpass rolling induces severe plastic deformation that recrystallizes coarse grains upon reheating by the subsequent pass.
results:
• Interpass rolling and ultrasonic excitation effectively transform tall columnar dendritic structures into equiaxed grains.
• Trailing gas shielding prevents oxidation-induced alpha-case formation in reactive titanium alloys.
• Deposition efficiency: GMAW/CMT (95–98%) > GTAW/PAW (85–90%).
• In-situ rolling at 50–100 kN reduces residual stress peaks by up to 60% and grain size by 50–70%.
• Tensile strength anisotropy across build orientations is reduced from >20% to <5% using optimized hybrid strategies.
future_work:
• Development of standardized multi-sensor closed-loop feedback systems combining optical cameras, pyrometry, and acoustic emission.
• Establishment of comprehensive fracture mechanics and fatigue crack propagation databases for hybrid-assisted WAAM components.
my_comments:
• Excellent global taxonomy of WAAM process interactions.
• Highlights the critical need to couple macro-thermal path models with microstructural evolution.

title: Comparative Thermal and Computational Analysis of the WAAM Process Using FEM and FDM Models with Experimental Validation
process_methodology: Comparative transient numerical modeling; 3D Implicit FEM (ANSYS) vs 3D Explicit/ADI FDM (Custom code); Goldak double-ellipsoid volumetric heat source; Multi-channel thermocouple and IR thermography validation.
key_params: Current: 120 A; Voltage: 19 V; Travel speed: 5 mm/s; Substrate: 200×100×6 mm; Heat efficiency: 0.80; Mesh: 1.0 mm uniform at bead, graded to 3.0 mm at boundaries; Latent heat: 270 kJ/kg.
observations:
• Formulated identical 3D transient heat conduction governing equations with temperature-dependent thermophysical properties for both FEM and FDM.
• FDM solves transient heat diffusion on structured Cartesian grids with exceptional computational speed via vectorized stencil operations.
• FEM excels at capturing curved bead profiles and complex boundary radiation losses with high local geometric fidelity.
• Temperature histories predicted by both numerical methods show close agreement in heating rates, peak temperatures, and cooling times.
• FDM slight underestimation of peak temperatures (<2.5%) arises from staircase approximations along curved bead crowns.
• High computational efficiency of FDM makes it uniquely suited for real-time digital twin monitoring and feedforward process control.
results:
• Both models accurately capture the trailing thermal comet-tail contour and inter-layer heat accumulation.
• Temperature-dependent convective/radiative boundary conditions dominate heat loss during cooling below 600°C.
• Peak temperature: Experimental = 1420°C, FEM = 1445°C (1.7% error), FDM = 1385°C (2.5% error).
• Cooling time t8/5 (800°C to 500°C): Experimental = 14.2 s, FEM = 14.8 s, FDM = 13.5 s.
• Total computational time for a 10-layer wall: FEM = 184 min, FDM = 41 min (FDM is 4.5× faster).
future_work:
• Developing curvilinear or immersed boundary FDM schemes to eliminate staircase approximations on complex geometric nodes.
• Coupling the fast FDM thermal solver with a real-time cellular automata or phase-field module for live grain size prediction.
my_comments:
• Directly demonstrates that FDM is viable for fast thermal prediction if geometry is simple.
• Can reach out to authors regarding their custom FDM solver implementation for potential benchmarking.

title: FEM Simulation Procedure for Distortion and Residual Stress Analysis of Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing
journal: IOP Conf. Series: Materials Science and Engineering, 455:012025
process_methodology: Sequentially coupled thermo-mechanical FEM in ABAQUS; Python-automated element birth-and-death via UEPACTIVATIONVOL; Temperature-dependent elastic-plastic constitutive law with isotropic hardening.
key_params: Substrate: 150×50×6 mm (cantilever clamped); 10-layer single-pass wall; Current: 110 A; Voltage: 18 V; Travel speed: 6 mm/s; Clamping released after cooling at t = 3600 s.
observations:
• High longitudinal tensile residual stresses develop at the deposit-substrate interface and the top deposited layers.
• Compressive residual stresses balance the tensile field within the interior and bottom regions of the substrate plate.
• Mechanical clamping during deposition restrains distortion but elevates the magnitude of accumulated plastic strain.
• Unclamping the component after complete room-temperature cooling releases elastic strain energy, causing immediate upward cantilever springback.
• Element activation strategy (birth-and-death) requires matching quiet element thermal conductivity to avoid artificial preheating ahead of the arc.
• Peak tensile residual stress approaches the room-temperature yield strength of the ER70S-6 weld metal (~380 MPa).
results:
• Deflection profile exhibits classic concave angular bending with maximum vertical displacement at the unconstrained cantilever tip.
• Residual stress distribution displays a sharp transition from high tension in the bead to compression in the substrate core.
• Maximum longitudinal tensile residual stress reached 368 MPa adjacent to the fusion line.
• Substrate core compressive stress stabilized at -145 MPa.
• Tip vertical deflection after unclamping measured 2.85 mm (FEA) vs. 3.12 mm (Experimental, 8.6% relative error).
future_work:
• Incorporating mixed kinematic-isotropic hardening to capture the Bauschinger effect during cyclic thermal loading.
• Implementing solid-state phase transformation volumetric expansion to refine fusion zone residual stress predictions.
my_comments:
• Standard procedural reference for ABAQUS element birth-and-death setup.
• Unclamping springback is the definitive test for validating the accumulated elastic strain energy.

title: Experimental and Numerical Thermal Monitoring of SS308L Structures Processed by Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing
process_methodology: 3D transient thermal FEM in COMSOL Multiphysics; Moving volumetric Gaussian-ellipsoid heat source; In-situ calibrated infrared thermography and contact thermopiles; Metallographic grain sizing.
key_params: Wire: 1.2 mm; Current: 130 A; Voltage: 19.5 V; Travel speed: 7.5 mm/s; Gas: Ar+2% CO2 (15 L/min); 15-layer thin wall; Interpass dwell: 60 s; Emissivity calibrated from 200°C to 1200°C.
observations:
• Calibrated temperature-dependent surface emissivity is essential for accurate quantitative non-contact IR thermography during WAAM.
• Heat accumulation across successive layers causes a progressive baseline temperature rise from layer 1 to layer 15.
• Diminished temperature gradient (G) in upper layers lowers the local cooling rate (G·R), widening the molten pool.
• Molten pool width expands by 1.8 mm from bottom to top layers due to reduced heat conduction into the preheated lower wall.
• Coarsening of secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) directly correlates with the simulated decline in local cooling rate.
• Interpass dwell time of 60 s is insufficient to achieve thermal steady state, leading to continuous heat buildup.
results:
• Thermal imaging captures the transition from conductive 3D heat sinking in the substrate to 2D planar heat flow in tall walls.
• Microstructure shows a pronounced transition from fine skeletal ferrite at bottom layers to coarse vermicular ferrite at upper layers.
• Base interpass temperature rose from 110°C (layer 2) to 345°C (layer 15).
• Cooling rate through 800°C dropped from 145°C/s at layer 1 down to 38°C/s at layer 15.
• Measured SDAS coarsened from 4.2 μm at the base to 8.9 μm at the top layer, matching thermal simulations with R² = 0.94.
future_work:
• Implementing an adaptive dwell-time algorithm that maintains a constant interpass temperature (<150°C) across all layers.
• Direct coupling of COMSOL local thermal histories with phase-field models to simulate dendritic arm coarsening.
my_comments:
• Excellent thermal calibration dataset for SS308L with synchronized IR thermography and contact thermocouples.
• Direct quantitative link between thermal simulation cooling rate and secondary dendrite arm spacing.

title: Numerical Modelling of Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing: Methods, Status, Trends, and Opportunities
journal: Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics, 54:273001
material: Multi-Material Overview (Steels, Titanium, Aluminum, Nickel Superalloys)
process_methodology: Comprehensive topical review; Multiscale physics classification: Microscopic (Phase-Field, CA), Mesoscopic (CFD, VOF, MHD), Macroscopic (FEM, Inherent Strain); Heat source model comparison.
key_params: Spatial scales: 10^-6 m (microstructure) to 10^-1 m (part-scale distortion); Time scales: 10^-5 s (droplet transfer) to 10^4 s (cooling); Heat sources: Goldak, double-ellipsoid, Gaussian, conical.
observations:
• Categorized WAAM numerical simulation into distinct temporal and spatial hierarchies across macro, meso, and micro scales.
• Macro-scale thermo-mechanical FEM is computationally prohibitive for meter-scale industrial parts without model reduction techniques.
• Inherent strain methods allow rapid distortion prediction by applying pre-calculated plastic strain tensors directly to elastic models.
• Meso-scale CFD-VOF models demonstrate that Marangoni convection and electromagnetic Lorentz forces dictate melt pool free-surface ripples.
• Microstructure models (Phase-Field and Cellular Automata) critically depend on accurate local thermal gradient (G) and growth velocity (R) inputs.
• Double-ellipsoid Goldak heat source remains the gold standard for arc processes due to flexible front/rear energy distribution calibration.
results:
• Marangoni flow direction (inward vs outward) governed by surface-active elements (S, O) dictates weld penetration depth.
• Columnar-to-equiaxed transition is strongly favored at the top center of the melt pool where G is lowest and R is highest.
• Inherent strain methods achieve 100× to 1000× computational speedup compared to transient thermo-elastic-plastic FEM.
• VOF free-surface simulations require sub-microsecond time steps (Δt < 10^-5 s) to maintain Courant number stability.
• Macro-FEM models typically capture global part distortion within 10–15% error of experimental CMM measurements.
future_work:
• Development of seamless, two-way coupled multiscale frameworks bridging atomistic phase-field kinetics with macro-FEM stress models.
• Physics-informed machine learning (PINN) surrogates to achieve real-time melt pool shape and thermal history prediction.
my_comments:
• Comprehensive reference for the simulation literature review chapter.
• Emphasizes why direct micro-macro coupling is computationally intractable without hierarchical homogenization.

title: Numerical Simulation of Molten Pool Behavior in Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing of Overhanging Structures Using Inconel 625
process_methodology: 3D transient CFD-VOF coupled with Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) in ANSYS Fluent; User-defined functions (UDF) for Marangoni traction, Lorentz forces, arc pressure, and gravity.
key_params: Overhang angles: 0°, 15°, 30°, 45°; Current: 110–140 A; Travel speed: 4–8 mm/s; Surface tension temperature coefficient dγ/dT = -0.35×10^-3 N/(m·K); Grid size: 0.1 mm near free surface; Time step: 10^-5 s.
observations:
• Gravitational force drives liquid metal runoff along the unsupported overhang edge as the inclination angle increases beyond 30°.
• Outward Marangoni flow combined with arc stagnation pressure flattens the molten pool and promotes edge humping.
• Increasing travel speed shortens the liquid lifetime of the molten pool, allowing surface tension to retain the overhang bead before sagging occurs.
• Tilting the welding torch at an angle opposing the overhang direction effectively utilizes arc pressure to push liquid metal upward.
• Heat dissipation is severely restricted in overhanging geometry due to reduced conductive contact area with the underlying substrate.
• Molten pool volume must be strictly throttled via low heat input to prevent catastrophic liquid metal dripping.
results:
• VOF fluid animations show severe molten pool edge sagging at 45° overhang when travel speed is below 5 mm/s.
• Optimized torch tilt and high travel speed produce stable, smooth overhanging wall boundaries without physical supports.
• Maximum stable unsupported overhang angle achieved: 45° at TS = 7.5 mm/s and I = 115 A.
• Liquid residence time above solidus reduced from 1.82 s (0° flat) down to 0.94 s (45° optimized overhang).
• Geometric edge profile deviation maintained within ±0.35 mm of the nominal CAD boundary.
future_work:
• Extending the CFD-VOF model to multi-layer (>5 layers) overhanging structures to capture cumulative heat buildup.
• Coupling the fluid dynamics model with microsegregation kinetics of Nb and Mo during Inconel 625 solidification.
my_comments:
• Fluid flow and surface tension dominate geometric stability in supportless overhanging WAAM.
• High travel speed is the primary operational parameter to prevent liquid metal sagging on overhangs.

title: Residual Stresses in Gas Tungsten Arc Welding: A Novel Phase-Field Thermo-Elastoplasticity Modeling and Parameter Treatment Framework
process_methodology: Coupled Phase-Field Thermo-Elastoplasticity (PFT-EP) variational framework; Leblond and Koistinen-Marburger solid-state phase transformation (SSPT) kinetics; Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP); Implicit FEM.
key_params: Austenite-to-martensite/bainite kinetics; Volumetric transformation expansion strain Δε_tr = 0.0085; Greenwood-Johnson TRIP parameter; Temperature-dependent phase yield strengths; Neutron diffraction validation.
observations:
• Solid-state phase transformation during cooling introduces a positive volumetric expansion that directly counteracts thermal contraction.
• Transformation expansion displaces the peak longitudinal tensile residual stress away from the weld centerline into the heat-affected zone.
• In materials undergoing martensitic or bainitic transformations, the fusion zone exhibits a distinct low-tensile or even compressive stress trough.
• Conventional thermo-elastic-plastic FE models that ignore phase transformations severely overestimate fusion line tensile residual stresses.
• Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) relaxes deviatoric stresses during phase change, significantly modifying the plastic strain field.
• Phase-field order parameters seamlessly track evolving metallurgical phase volume fractions across continuous thermal cycles.
results:
• Predicted residual stress contours show a characteristic 'M-shaped' longitudinal stress profile with a valley in the weld center.
• Phase-field formulation captures diffuse metallurgical boundaries between parent ferrite, HAZ bainite, and fusion martensite.
• Fusion zone peak tensile stress with SSPT dropped to 180 MPa compared to 440 MPa in models neglecting phase transformation.
• Peak tensile stress shifted into the adjacent HAZ at a magnitude of 320 MPa.
• Simulated residual stress profiles matched neutron diffraction measurements within 12% across the entire cross-section.
future_work:
• Adapting the variational PFT-EP framework to multi-pass WAAM with cyclic re-austenitization and tempering.
• Calibrating phase-field transformation parameters for multi-component alloys using in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction.
my_comments:
• Crucial proof that neglecting solid-state phase transformation invalidates steel residual stress simulations.
• The M-shaped residual stress profile is a classic signature of martensitic/bainitic transformation expansion.

title: Effect of Interpass Temperature on Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing of Ti-6Al-4V Alloy: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties
process_methodology: GTAW-based WAAM; Trailing ultra-pure argon shielding enclosure; Interpass temperature regulation via non-contact infrared pyrometer; EBSD, SEM, Vickers microhardness, tensile testing.
key_params: Interpass temperatures: 50°C, 100°C, 150°C, 200°C; Wire: 1.2 mm; Current: 140 A; Travel speed: 120 mm/min; 25-layer walls; Substrate: Ti-6Al-4V plate (12 mm thick); Beta-transus temperature: ~995°C.
observations:
• Maintaining a low interpass temperature (50–100°C) accelerates cooling through the beta-transus (~995°C), refining the transformed alpha microstructure.
• Low interpass temperature produces a fine basketweave (Widmanstätten) alpha+beta colony morphology with high dislocation density.
• Elevated interpass temperature (200°C) extends the dwell time in the high-temperature beta phase, promoting severe epitaxial grain growth.
• Prior-beta columnar grains span across multiple deposited layers (reaching lengths >5 mm) along the vertical thermal gradient.
• High interpass temperature coarsens alpha-lath thickness and thickens continuous grain boundary alpha (GB-alpha) films.
• Tensile strength decreases systematically with increasing interpass temperature, while ductility exhibits a moderate increase.
results:
• 50°C interpass yields fine basketweave alpha colonies that effectively impede dislocation glide.
• 200°C interpass promotes coarse parallel alpha-plate colonies and continuous GB-alpha that facilitate planar slip.
• At 50°C interpass: YS = 910±14 MPa, UTS = 995±12 MPa, Elongation = 9.2%, Hardness = 355 HV.
• At 200°C interpass: YS = 840±18 MPa, UTS = 925±15 MPa, Elongation = 13.5%, Hardness = 322 HV.
• Alpha-lath thickness increased from 0.85±0.12 μm at 50°C to 2.42±0.28 μm at 200°C.
future_work:
• High-cycle fatigue and fracture toughness testing as a function of alpha-lath aspect ratio and GB-alpha thickness.
• Evaluating post-deposition beta-annealing and sub-transus aging heat treatments to eliminate directional anisotropy.
my_comments:
• Clear metallurgical proof that controlling interpass temperature is equivalent to tailoring alpha-lath width in Ti-6Al-4V.
• Trade-off between build time (longer cooling wait) and mechanical tensile strength must be optimized.

title: Effect of Heat Input on Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Ti-6Al-4V Alloy Fabricated by Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing
process_methodology: Plasma Arc (PAW) and Gas Tungsten Arc (GTAW) WAAM; Argon inert gas containment box; EBSD orientation analysis; Optical metallography; Longitudinal and transverse tensile testing.
key_params: Heat input range: 0.35 kJ/mm to 1.25 kJ/mm; Wire feed speed: 1.0–2.5 m/min; Travel speed: 150–400 mm/min; Current: 100–220 A; Wire diameter: 1.2 mm.
observations:
• Prior-beta grains grow epitaxially from the substrate, exhibiting a strong <001> crystallographic fiber texture aligned with the maximum heat flux.
• Increasing heat input significantly widens the prior-beta columnar grains due to prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures.
• Transformed alpha-phase morphology shifts from fine interwoven basketweave to coarse aligned colony packets with increasing heat input.
• Continuous grain boundary alpha (GB-alpha) films thicken at high heat input, serving as preferential crack initiation and propagation paths.
• Low heat input restricts prior-beta grain widening and promotes high nucleation density of intra-granular alpha laths.
• Anisotropy in tensile properties is minimized at low heat input due to the finer, more randomly oriented alpha colonies.
results:
• EBSD reconstructions confirm epitaxial beta grain growth across dozens of layer interfaces without nucleation of new grains.
• Tensile fracture surfaces at high heat input display intergranular facets along prior-beta boundaries decorated by GB-alpha.
• Prior-beta columnar grain width expanded from 0.45±0.08 mm at 0.35 kJ/mm to 1.82±0.22 mm at 1.25 kJ/mm.
• Maximum UTS of 980 MPa achieved at 0.35 kJ/mm, dropping to 895 MPa at 1.25 kJ/mm.
• Tensile strength anisotropy ratio (Horizontal/Vertical) varied from 1.04 at low heat input to 1.18 at high heat input.
future_work:
• Investigating in-situ micro-alloying with boron or yttrium to break prior-beta columnar grain epitaxy during arc deposition.
• Evaluating high-pressure interpass rolling to induce dynamic recrystallization of coarse prior-beta grains.
my_comments:
• Classic, highly-cited foundational paper on Ti-6Al-4V WAAM metallurgy.
• Demonstrates why high heat input is detrimental to fracture toughness and tensile isotropy in titanium.

title: Experimental Investigations on Mechanical Properties of Multi-Layered Structure Fabricated by GMAW-Based WAAM of SS316L
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance, 31:4812–4825
process_methodology: GMAW-based WAAM; Synergic pulsed arc mode; Ar+2% CO2 shielding; Multi-directional tensile testing (0° horizontal, 45° diagonal, 90° vertical); Charpy V-notch impact testing at 20°C and -40°C; EBSD and SEM-EDS.
key_params: Wire: 1.2 mm; Current: 120–160 A; Voltage: 18–21 V; Travel speed: 250–350 mm/min; 30-layer wall and block structures; Interpass temperature: 120°C; Substrate: SS304 plate.
observations:
• Microstructure consists of an austenitic (gamma) matrix with 5.5–8.2% residual delta-ferrite retained at cellular-dendritic boundaries.
• Microsegregation of chromium and molybdenum into the inter-dendritic liquid stabilizes skeletal and vermicular delta-ferrite networks.
• Strong <001> fiber texture develops parallel to the vertical build direction due to steep directional heat extraction.
• Tensile properties in all three directions (0°, 45°, 90°) exceed standard wrought ASTM A240 requirements.
• Vertical tensile specimens exhibit lower yield strength but superior elongation compared to horizontal specimens.
• Cryogenic Charpy impact toughness remains exceptionally high due to the high intrinsic ductility of the FCC austenite matrix.
results:
• Inter-dendritic delta-ferrite acts as an effective crack arrester, branching microcracks during plastic deformation.
• SEM fractography shows fine, uniform equiaxed dimples indicative of classic ductile microvoid coalescence.
• Yield Strength: 340–375 MPa; Ultimate Tensile Strength: 590–625 MPa across all orientations.
• Elongation: 42% (Horizontal), 48% (Diagonal), 54% (Vertical build direction).
• Charpy impact toughness: 115 J at 20°C and 88 J at -40°C; Microhardness: 185–205 HV0.5 across all 30 layers.
future_work:
• Long-term electrochemical pitting and crevice corrosion testing in acidified ferric chloride (ASTM G48) media.
• High-temperature tensile and creep rupture testing up to 650°C for nuclear and petrochemical pressure vessel applications.
my_comments:
• Comprehensive mechanical baseline for SS316L WAAM exceeding wrought material standards.
• Strong ductility in vertical samples is explained by loading parallel to elongated columnar grain boundaries.

title: Mechanical Properties, Microstructural Characteristics and Heat Treatment Effects of WAAM Stainless-Steel Plate Material
process_methodology: CMT-WAAM (Fronius); Synchrotron X-ray Diffraction (SXRD); Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM); EBSD; Post-weld heat treatment (Solution treatment at 1040°C + Peak aging H900 at 480°C / Overaging H1150 at 620°C).
key_params: Deposition rate: 2.4 kg/h; Current: 150 A; TS: 400 mm/min; Solution annealing: 1040°C for 1 h (argon/water quench); Aging H900: 480°C for 1 h; Aging H1150: 620°C for 4 h.
observations:
• As-built 17-4 PH exhibits hierarchical lath martensite containing ~12% retained austenite and un-dissolved copper clusters.
• Intrinsic cyclic reheating during deposition creates inhomogeneous hardness gradients (310–360 HV) due to partial in-situ tempering.
• Direct aging without prior solution treatment fails to achieve peak hardness due to uneven solute distribution in as-built martensite.
• Solution treatment at 1040°C fully homogenizes the alloy, dissolves retained austenite, and creates a uniform supersaturated martensite matrix.
• Subsequent H900 aging precipitates highly coherent, nanoscale copper-rich clusters (2–5 nm) that provide intense precipitation strengthening.
• Overaging at H1150 (620°C) coarsens copper precipitates and promotes reverted austenite formation, significantly boosting ductility.
results:
• TEM bright-field images reveal dense dislocation networks in as-built lath martensite, transitioning to uniform Cu-precipitates after H900 aging.
• Synchrotron XRD confirms complete elimination of retained austenite after 1040°C solution annealing and water quenching.
• As-built: YS = 780 MPa, UTS = 1050 MPa, Elongation = 12%, Hardness = 330 HV.
• Solution + H900 Aging: YS = 1180 MPa, UTS = 1320 MPa, Elongation = 10.5%, Hardness = 435 HV.
• Solution + H1150 Overaging: YS = 890 MPa, UTS = 1010 MPa, Elongation = 18%, Hardness = 345 HV.
future_work:
• Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) susceptibility evaluation in marine environments under peak-aged and over-aged conditions.
• Plane-strain fracture toughness (K_IC) testing across different post-weld heat treatment regimens.
my_comments:
• Excellent demonstration that post-weld solutionizing is mandatory for precipitation-hardening steels before aging.
• Reaches outstanding tensile strength (>1300 MPa) in WAAM 17-4 PH.

title: Integrated Experimental and Simulation Approach to Establish the Effect of Elemental Segregation in Inconel 718 Welds
process_methodology: GTAW arc welding and cladding; Scheil-Gulliver solidification modeling and DICTRA 1D multi-component diffusion simulation coupled with Thermo-Calc CALPHAD databases; EPMA/WDS microprobe line scanning.
key_params: Cooling rates: 10 K/s to 1000 K/s; Nominal Nb: 5.12 wt%; Partition coefficient k_Nb = 0.48; Laves phase eutectic temperature T_eut = 1160°C; DICTRA cylindrical cell size: 5–25 μm.
observations:
• Niobium strongly segregates to the inter-dendritic liquid phase during solidification due to its low partition coefficient (k_Nb ≈ 0.48).
• As solidification fraction exceeds 0.95, inter-dendritic liquid Nb concentration reaches 18–22 wt%.
• Extreme Nb enrichment triggers the terminal eutectic precipitation of brittle Laves phase (η-(Ni,Fe,Cr)2(Nb,Ti,Mo)) and NbC carbides.
• Formation of Laves phase severely depletes Nb from the gamma matrix, preventing subsequent precipitation of strengthening γ'' (Ni3Nb) phases.
• Solid-state back-diffusion of Nb during weld cooling is negligible due to its slow diffusion coefficient in the FCC nickel matrix.
• High-temperature homogenization heat treatment (>1100°C) is mandatory to dissolve Laves phase and redistribute Nb back into solid solution.
results:
• BSE micrographs reveal continuous, interconnected chains of brittle white Laves phase along inter-dendritic boundaries in as-cast state.
• DICTRA diffusion models accurately simulate the progressive homogenization of Nb concentration profiles during isothermal soaking.
• Inter-dendritic Nb concentration reached a peak of 19.4 wt% (vs. 5.12 wt% nominal matrix composition).
• As-solidified Laves phase volume fraction measured between 3.2% and 5.8%.
• Homogenization at 1150°C for 2 h reduced inter-dendritic Nb peak concentration below 6.0 wt%, fully dissolving the Laves phase.
future_work:
• Extending DICTRA 1D microsegregation simulations to 2D/3D phase-field models incorporating anisotropic dendritic tip kinetics.
• Investigating the effect of cyclic thermal reheating during multi-pass WAAM on in-situ Laves phase coarsening and liquation cracking.
my_comments:
• Foundational reference for microsegregation in Inconel 718.
• Explains why post-WAAM homogenization is critical before applying standard double-aging treatments (720°C/620°C).

title: High-Throughput Experiment and Numerical Simulation to Study Solidification Cracking in 2195 Aluminum Alloy Welds
process_methodology: Variable-polarity GTAW (VP-GTAW); High-throughput Transverse Varestraint cracking testing with synchronized high-speed imaging; Scheil-Gulliver solidification modeling in Thermo-Calc; Kou cracking criterion |dT/d(fs^1/2)|.
key_params: Augmented mechanical strain: 1.0%, 2.0%, 4.0%; Solidification temperature range ΔT = 135 K; Critical temperature range for cracking: solid fraction fs = 0.85 to 0.98; Filler wires: ER2319 (Al-Cu), ER4043 (Al-Si), ER5356 (Al-Mg).
observations:
• Al-Li 2195 alloy exhibits extreme susceptibility to solidification hot cracking due to its wide freezing temperature range (ΔT ≈ 135 K).
• Near the end of solidification (0.85 < fs < 0.98), low-melting terminal eutectic liquid films (Al+Al2Cu+Al2CuLi) coat dendritic grain boundaries.
• Inter-dendritic liquid permeability drops drastically in the critical temperature range, preventing liquid feeding under thermal tensile strains.
• The maximum value of the Kou cracking criterion index |dT/d(fs^1/2)| near fs = 0.99 accurately predicts hot cracking susceptibility.
• Introducing ER2319 filler wire (6.3 wt% Cu) modifies melt pool composition, increasing the volume of eutectic liquid to heal propagating cracks.
• Inoculation with Zr/Ti promotes heterogeneous grain nucleation, producing fine equiaxed grains that accommodate tensile strain without tearing.
results:
• High-speed video shows hot cracks initiating in the mushy zone behind the melt pool trailing edge and propagating along columnar boundaries.
• Addition of ER2319 filler transforms coarse columnar grains into fine equiaxed grains, completely suppressing centerline cracking.
• Total Crack Length (TCL) in autogenous 2195 weld reached 18.5 mm at 4% augmented strain.
• Using ER2319 filler reduced TCL down to 3.2 mm (an 82.7% reduction in cracking susceptibility).
• The maximum Kou cracking index |dT/d(fs^1/2)| dropped from 385 K (autogenous 2195) to 112 K (2195 + ER2319).
future_work:
• Incorporating nanoparticle grain refiners (e.g., TiC, TiB2) into Al-Li wire to achieve crack-free autogenous WAAM.
• Formulating a 2D phase-field model coupled with mechanical stress to simulate dynamic crack initiation in the mushy zone.
my_comments:
• Solidification cracking index |dT/d(fs^1/2)| is a powerful theoretical metric for evaluating filler wire compatibility.
• Direct relevance to hot tearing prevention in 2xxx and 7xxx aluminum WAAM.

title: Multi-Material Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing of Low and High Alloyed Aluminium Alloys with In-Situ Material Analysis
process_methodology: Dual-wire CMT-WAAM system with synchronized wire feed switching; In-situ Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS); 10-layer linear compositional gradient FGM; EBSD, EDX, microhardness, tensile testing.
key_params: Wire diameter: 1.2 mm; CMT Advanced arc mode; Travel speed: 600 mm/min; WFS: 4.5–7.0 m/min; Interpass temp: 80°C; LIBS laser: 1064 nm Nd:YAG (10 mJ/pulse, 20 Hz); 20-layer walls.
observations:
• Direct, abrupt joining of Al-Si and Al-Mg alloys generates coarse, brittle script-like Mg2Si intermetallic phases at the transition boundary.
• Brittle Mg2Si intermetallics cause severe interfacial embrittlement and catastrophic premature delamination under tensile loading.
• Designing a continuous 10-layer linear compositional gradient refines Mg2Si into homogeneously dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
• In-situ LIBS spectroscopy provides real-time elemental quantification of Si and Mg in the molten pool during deposition.
• Dynamic adjustment of individual wire feed speeds enables precise local compositional tailoring on a layer-by-layer basis.
• The functionally graded transition zone achieves higher tensile strength than both parent monolithic aluminum alloys.
results:
• In-situ LIBS spectra accurately track real-time emission line intensity ratios (Mg I 285.2 nm / Si I 288.1 nm) in the arc plume.
• Microstructure transitions smoothly from primary alpha-Al + Al-Si eutectic to dense nanoscale Mg2Si-strengthened alpha-Al matrix.
• In-situ LIBS measured local Mg and Si concentrations within 4.5% deviation from calibrated EPMA microprobe measurements.
• Hardness peaked at the transition zone at 115 HV0.1 (due to Mg2Si dispersion) vs. 65 HV (AlSi5) and 78 HV (AlMg5).
• Tensile strength of the functionally graded transition achieved 265 MPa, exceeding both parent alloys.
future_work:
• Implementing real-time closed-loop feedback control where LIBS signal dynamically adjusts wire feed rates to correct composition drifts.
• High-cycle fatigue testing of the graded Al-Si/Al-Mg interface under cyclic bending loads.
my_comments:
• Superb demonstration of in-situ spectroscopy integrated with multi-material WAAM.
• Proves that controlled compositional grading can turn a brittle intermetallic (Mg2Si) into a strengthening asset.

title: Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing of Multi-Material Parts Using H-13 Tool Steel and SS304 Stainless Steel
material: AISI H13 Tool Steel + AISI 304 Austenitic Stainless Steel
process_methodology: Multi-material GMAW/GTAW WAAM; Substrate preheating at 300°C; Post-Weld Heat Treatment (Double tempering at 560°C for 2 h); Pin-on-disk dry sliding wear testing; SEM-EDS line mapping; Interfacial shear testing.
key_params: Wires: 1.2 mm; Current: 120–150 A; Travel speed: 180 mm/min; Interpass temperature: 250–300°C; Preheating: 300°C; Tempering: 560°C / 2h + 560°C / 2h; Substrate: Structural steel plate.
observations:
• Fabricated bimetallic components featuring a ductile, corrosion-resistant SS304 core and a wear-resistant H13 tool steel functional surface.
• Direct deposition of high-hardenability H13 steel onto cold substrate results in severe martensitic cold cracking due to extreme transformation stresses.
• Substrate preheating to 300°C combined with an intermediate SS304 austenitic buffer layer completely prevents cracking.
• Strong chemical potential gradients drive carbon and alloying elements (Cr, Mo, V) to diffuse across the H13/SS304 interface.
• Austenitic SS304 buffer layer accommodates thermal expansion mismatch and blunts propagating residual stress concentrations.
• Double tempering at 560°C transforms retained austenite and precipitates secondary alloy carbides in the H13 layer.
results:
• Defect-free, fully dense metallurgical bond across the H13/SS304 transition without porosity or lack of fusion.
• Microstructure transitions from austenitic dendrites (SS304) to tempered lath martensite decorated with secondary carbides (H13).
• H13 surface hardness reached 58–62 HRC (650–720 HV) after double tempering.
• SS304 buffer layer maintained 210–230 HV with elongation exceeding 45%.
• Wear volume loss of the bimetallic H13 surface was 82% lower than monolithic structural steel; interfacial shear strength exceeded 420 MPa.
future_work:
• Thermal fatigue and thermal shock testing simulating high-pressure die casting service cycles (room temp to 600°C).
• Residual stress mapping across the dissimilar interface using neutron diffraction.
my_comments:
• Highly practical industrial concept: tough stainless steel core with hard tool steel working layer.
• Preheating to 300°C is mandatory to suppress martensitic cracking in H13 tool steel.

title: Multi-Material Design in Additive Manufacturing — Feasibility and Process Validation for Industrial Applications
journal: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing, 6(4):88
process_methodology: Design and feasibility screening matrix for multi-material AM; DED-Arc / WAAM and Powder DED process trials; Non-destructive testing (Ultrasonic + Industrial X-ray CT); Metallurgical compatibility modeling.
key_params: Evaluated dissimilar combinations based on: thermal expansion mismatch (Δα), solid solubility limits, liquidus-solidus freezing ranges, formation enthalpy (ΔH_mix), and intermetallic formation tendencies.
observations:
• Established a systematic decision-tree framework to evaluate metallurgical feasibility before attempting multi-material AM.
• Identified three primary physical failure mechanisms in dissimilar alloy deposition: (1) hot cracking, (2) solid-state cold cracking, and (3) brittle IMC formation.
• Solidification cracking dominates in alloy pairs with wide liquidus-solidus separation and poor inter-dendritic liquid feeding.
• Coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatch (Δα) creates intense interfacial shear stresses during cooling, driving delamination.
• Direct dissimilar deposition is unviable when CTE mismatch exceeds 25% (Δα > 4×10^-6 /K) without intermediate buffer layers.
• Stepwise functionally graded transitions effectively redistribute shear stresses across multiple intermediate layer planes.
results:
• X-ray CT scans reveal severe interfacial delamination in unbuffered Steel-Bronze joints, which is completely eliminated using a 3-layer nickel buffer.
• Metallographic screening accurately correlates phase diagram eutectic/peritectic reactions with observed weldability.
• Interfacial defect and crack rate dropped from 65% in direct dissimilar joints down to <2% with a 3-layer graded buffer.
• Formulated the empirical design rule: Δα / α_base < 25% for crack-free direct arc deposition.
• Multi-material joint shear strength recovered up to 90% of the weaker parent alloy when buffer layers were employed.
future_work:
• Developing an automated CALPHAD-based computational tool to calculate optimal multi-element buffer pathways directly from thermodynamic databases.
• Standardization of qualification protocols for additively manufactured multi-material components in aerospace and defense.
my_comments:
• Comprehensive roadmap for evaluating whether two alloys can be joined via WAAM.
• The 25% CTE mismatch criterion is an essential design rule for multi-material thesis chapters.

title: Application of Ultrasonic Vibrations in Welding and Metal Processing: A Status Review
material: Overview across Aluminum, Magnesium, Titanium, and Steel Alloys
process_methodology: Comprehensive status review; Acoustic physics of molten pools; Acoustic cavitation, acoustic streaming, radiation pressure; Application across Arc welding (GMAW, GTAW), casting, and additive manufacturing.
key_params: Ultrasonic frequencies: 20–60 kHz; Vibration amplitudes: 5–50 μm; Acoustic power: 100–2000 W; Coupling methods: substrate horn, direct melt pool sonotrode, wire excitation.
observations:
• Acoustic cavitation generates localized transient high temperatures (>5000 K) and extreme shockwave pressures (>1000 atm) upon bubble implosion.
• Cavitation shockwaves mechanically fracture fragile growing columnar dendrite arms in the mushy zone.
• Fragmented dendritic debris is transported throughout the melt pool by acoustic streaming, acting as abundant heterogeneous nuclei.
• Proliferation of fragmented nuclei triggers a complete Columnar-to-Equiaxed Transition (CET) without chemical inoculant additions.
• Acoustic streaming (bulk Eckart flow) accelerates liquid mixing, homogenizes temperature, and eliminates solute macrosegregation.
• Ultrasonic vibrations force dissolved gas bubbles (hydrogen) to oscillate, coalesce via Bjerknes forces, and rapidly escape the melt pool.
results:
• Microstructural comparison across diverse alloy systems proves universal transformation of columnar grains into fine equiaxed structures.
• Radiographic and CT scans confirm near-total suppression of gas porosity in aluminum and magnesium welds.
• Average grain size refined by 50% to 85% across Al, Mg, and steel weldments under resonant ultrasonic excitation.
• Porosity volume fraction reduced by up to 90% due to cavitation-assisted bubble degassing.
• Residual tensile stresses reduced by 30% to 60% through acoustic stress relaxation and uniform thermal dissipation.
future_work:
• High-temperature acoustic waveguide design to maintain resonant frequency coupling across evolving tall 3D WAAM structures.
• Direct numerical simulation of multi-bubble acoustic cavitation coupled with Navier-Stokes melt pool equations.
my_comments:
• Foundational review of ultrasonic physical mechanisms in liquid metal processing.
• Cavitation-induced dendrite fragmentation and acoustic streaming are the two dominant physical mechanisms.

title: In Situ Observation of Melt Pool Evolution in Ultrasonic Vibration-Assisted Directed Energy Deposition
process_methodology: Ultrasonic vibration-assisted Directed Energy Deposition (UVA-DED / WAAM); In-situ high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging (20,000 fps); Synchronized high-speed optical videography; EBSD orientation analysis.
key_params: Ultrasonic frequency: 28 kHz; Amplitude: 10–25 μm; Laser/Arc power: 800–1400 W; Substrate: Piezoelectric transducer attached to bottom center; Frame rate: 20,000 fps; Spatial resolution: 2 μm/pixel.
observations:
• Synchrotron X-ray imaging directly captures real-time acoustic cavitation bubble dynamics and melt pool flow fields in operando.
• Ultrasonic excitation generates high-frequency surface Faraday waves and accelerates acoustic streaming flow.
• Cavitation bubble collapse near the advancing solidification front physically shatters growing secondary dendritic arms within milliseconds.
• Trapped gas pores oscillate violently under acoustic pressure cycles, coalescing into larger bubbles that rapidly float to the surface.
• Intense acoustic streaming thoroughly homogenizes the thermal field, collapsing the high thermal gradient G at the melt pool bottom.
• EBSD mapping confirms complete transition from epitaxial columnar grains to random equiaxed grain structures.
results:
• Direct synchrotron video proof of cavitation-driven dendrite fragmentation and instantaneous gas pore expulsion.
• Complete suppression of tall epitaxial <001> columnar grains in Inconel 718 deposits.
• Melt pool fluid flow velocity increased from 0.18 m/s (without US) to 0.62 m/s (with US, ~3× faster than Marangoni flow).
• Gas pore upward escape velocity accelerated by 4.2×, reducing residual porosity from 1.4% to <0.08%.
• Grain aspect ratio reduced from 6.8 (columnar) down to 1.3 (equiaxed).
future_work:
• Multi-layer wall synchrotron experiments to evaluate acoustic wave transmission attenuation across successive build layers.
• Quantitative particle image velocimetry (PIV) analysis of synchrotron frames to map exact acoustic streaming shear stress tensors.
my_comments:
• Definitive experimental synchrotron proof of ultrasonic cavitation and pore degassing in additive manufacturing.
• Directly demonstrates that acoustic streaming velocity easily overwhelms natural Marangoni convection.

title: Ultrasonic-Assisted Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing Significantly Improves Impact Toughness of 5183 Aluminum Alloy
process_methodology: Variable Polarity CMT-WAAM (VP-CMT); Ultrasonic vibration applied to substrate plate (20 kHz, 1.2 kW); 3D X-ray Computed Tomography (XCT); EBSD, TEM; Tensile and Charpy V-notch impact tests at 20°C and -40°C.
key_params: Ultrasonic power: 0 W, 400 W, 800 W, 1200 W; Frequency: 20 kHz; Travel speed: 500 mm/min; WFS: 6.5 m/min; 20-layer walls; Substrate: 5083 plate.
observations:
• Applied substrate ultrasonic vibration during VP-CMT deposition of 5183 aluminum alloy across varying acoustic power levels.
• Ultrasonic power at 1200 W completely shatters coarse columnar grains, achieving full grain refinement across all 20 layers.
• Acoustic streaming promotes uniform distribution of nanoscale β-Mg2Al3 precipitates, preventing grain boundary film embrittlement.
• 3D XCT reconstructions demonstrate dramatic reduction in total hydrogen pore count and average pore diameter.
• Fine equiaxed grain boundaries effectively deflect propagating microcracks during dynamic impact loading.
• Overcomes the conventional trade-off between strength and impact toughness in aluminum additive manufacturing.
results:
• Grain structure transforms from coarse epitaxial columnar grains (aspect ratio >10) into isotropic equiaxed grains.
• Charpy fracture surfaces shift from low-energy intergranular tearing to high-energy transgranular dimpled rupture.
• Charpy impact energy at 20°C increased from 24.5 J (without US) to 43.2 J at 1200 W (a 76.3% increase).
• Low-temperature (-40°C) impact energy reached 38.5 J.
• Average grain size refined from 84.5 μm to 21.3 μm; porosity volume fraction dropped from 0.82% down to 0.09%.
• UTS increased from 285 MPa to 318 MPa with elongation rising from 18.5% to 26.2%.
future_work:
• Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) testing in 3.5% NaCl solution to verify the corrosion resistance of uniformly dispersed β-Mg2Al3 phase.
• Developing a toolhead-mounted ultrasonic excitation system to allow unlimited component build heights.
my_comments:
• Outstanding proof of ultrasonic assistance simultaneously enhancing strength, ductility, and cryogenic toughness.
• 76% boost in impact toughness makes WAAM 5xxx aluminum fully competitive with forged aerospace components.

title: Microstructure and Properties of 316L Stainless Steel Fabricated by Ultrasonic Impact and External Wire Feeding-Assisted Tandem Wire and Arc Additive Manufacturing
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
process_methodology: Tandem-wire GMAW-WAAM (dual arc) + Auxiliary cold wire feed + Interpass Ultrasonic Impact Treatment (UIT); XRD residual stress (sin²ψ method); HR-EBSD, TEM; Potentiodynamic polarization corrosion testing in 3.5% NaCl.
key_params: Primary tandem wires: 1.2 mm each; Cold wire: 1.0 mm; Deposition rate: 4.85 kg/h; UIT frequency: 20 kHz; UIT amplitude: 35 μm; UIT travel speed: 100 mm/min; 15-layer thick plate structures.
observations:
• Tandem-wire arc configuration combined with cold wire feeding achieves ultra-high deposition rates exceeding 4.8 kg/h.
• Auxiliary cold wire absorbs excess arc heat, maintaining thermal control despite the high deposition rate.
• Interlayer UIT peening introduces severe plastic deformation (SPD) in a ~50 μm deep subsurface layer, creating dense dislocation tangles.
• Re-melting of the severely deformed SPD layer by the subsequent pass provides abundant heterogeneous nucleation sites, eliminating columnar grains.
• Interpass UIT converts high tensile residual stresses into deep compressive residual stresses.
• Compressive surface stresses and refined grain boundaries significantly enhance electrochemical pitting corrosion resistance.
results:
• HR-EBSD confirms complete suppression of columnar grain epitaxy, producing an ultra-fine equiaxed recrystallized grain structure.
• TEM reveals dense dislocation walls and planar dislocation arrays generated by high-frequency ultrasonic impact peening.
• Deposition rate reached 4.85 kg/h (more than 2.5× higher than standard single-wire GMAW-WAAM).
• Surface residual stress converted from +280 MPa (tensile, without UIT) to -385 MPa (compressive, with UIT).
• Yield strength increased from 345 MPa to 465 MPa (34.8% increase) while preserving 45% elongation.
• Pitting corrosion potential (E_pit) in 3.5% NaCl increased by +140 mV.
future_work:
• Robotic automation of synchronized tandem-wire deposition and trailing UIT toolpaths for continuous, non-stop manufacturing.
• High-cycle fatigue and corrosion-fatigue testing under cyclic tensile-compression loading.
my_comments:
• Exemplary industrial hybrid manufacturing concept: high productivity (4.85 kg/h) + mechanical surface enhancement (UIT).
• Deep compressive stress (-385 MPa) combined with higher yield strength is ideal for fatigue-critical structures.

title: Review: The Metal Additive-Manufacturing Technology of the Ultrasonic-Assisted Wire-and-Arc Additive-Manufacturing Process
material: Review across Titanium, Aluminum, Stainless Steel, and Nickel Superalloys
process_methodology: Systematic review of Ultrasonic-Assisted WAAM (UA-WAAM); Classification of transducer coupling configurations; Physical mechanisms (cavitation, acoustic streaming, thermal effect); Mechanical property and stress relief synthesis.
key_params: Coupling modes: Substrate vibration, direct molten pool immersion, ultrasonic wire vibration, interlayer ultrasonic impact peening (UIP/UIT); Frequency: 20–40 kHz; Power: 0.5–2.5 kW.
observations:
• UA-WAAM resolves the fundamental bottlenecks of conventional WAAM: coarse columnar grains, strong texture anisotropy, tensile residual stress, and pores.
• Cavitation-induced dendrite fragmentation is the primary driver of Columnar-to-Equiaxed Transition (CET).
• Direct molten pool acoustic coupling provides maximum grain refinement but requires specialized refractory sonotrode tips.
• Substrate ultrasonic vibration is easiest to implement industrially but suffers acoustic wave attenuation as part height exceeds 100 mm.
• Trailing ultrasonic impact treatment (UIT) is the most effective approach for eliminating tensile residual stresses and inducing compressive layers.
• Ultrasonic vibration promotes uniform dispersion of secondary reinforcing phases and accelerates hydrogen bubble outgassing.
results:
• Grain structure shifts from anisotropic columnar prior-beta/austenite grains to fine isotropic equiaxed grain networks.
• Radiographic inspection confirms order-of-magnitude reduction in gas pores across light alloys.
• Yield and tensile strength improved by 15% to 35% across aluminum and titanium alloys.
• Ductility (elongation to failure) increased by 20% to 50% due to grain boundary tortuosity.
• Average grain size refined by up to 75%; residual tensile stresses reduced by >50%.
future_work:
• Development of adaptive resonance-tracking ultrasonic generators that compensate for temperature-dependent acoustic velocity shifts.
• Integration of multi-axis robotic trailing UIT heads for complex 3D non-planar toolpaths.
my_comments:
• Excellent state-of-the-art review classifying all ultrasonic WAAM hardware configurations.
• Distinguishes between in-situ liquid cavitation (grain refinement) and post-solidification UIT (compressive stress generation).

title: Monte-Carlo-Assisted Phase Field Simulations of Grain Structure Evolution in Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing
process_methodology: Hybrid multiscale model: Macro FEM thermal history -> Mesoscopic Multi-Phase-Field (MPF) for dendritic solidification -> Potts Monte Carlo (MC) for solid-state grain growth during multi-pass reheating.
key_params: Thermal gradient G = 10^4–10^6 K/m; Solidification rate R = 1–20 mm/s; 36 non-conserved orientation order parameters η_i; Grain boundary mobility M_GB; Grain boundary energy γ_GB = 0.6 J/m².
observations:
• Solidification grain morphology in WAAM is primarily governed by the ratio G/R (morphological stability) and product G·R (cooling rate).
• Epitaxial growth dominates at the fusion boundary where substrate grains with <001> easy-growth axes aligned with heat flux outgrow misoriented grains.
• Thermal reheating from subsequent passes triggers solid-state grain boundary migration, causing significant grain coarsening in the HAZ.
• Columnar-to-equiaxed transition occurs when heterogeneous nucleation ahead of the solidification front reaches a critical particle density.
• Multi-phase-field accurately simulates competitive dendritic overgrowth and crystallographic texture evolution during single-track solidification.
• Potts Monte Carlo module efficiently captures solid-state recrystallization and normal grain growth during cyclic multi-layer reheating.
results:
• Phase-field simulations reveal competitive growth where favorably oriented <001> dendritic arms pinch off misaligned neighbors.
• Grain aspect ratio evolves from high elongation (>10) in pure columnar regimes to near-unity (~1.5) in equiaxed zones.
• CET boundary established at G^3.4 / R < 1.2×10^5 K^3.4·s/m^4.4 with heterogeneous nucleant density N_0 > 10^12 m^-3.
• Average grain size in the re-heated HAZ coarsened by 45% compared to the as-solidified dendritic state.
• Predicted grain morphology map matched experimental EBSD pole figures across diverse G and R processing windows.
future_work:
• Incorporating fluid convection (Marangoni flow) into the phase-field module to capture flow-induced grain deflection.
• Extending from 36 discrete orientation states to continuous quaternion-based 3D crystallographic orientation space.
my_comments:
• Direct methodological blueprint for coupling macroscopic thermal FEM with mesoscopic phase-field grain growth.

title: The Interaction between Grains during Columnar-to-Equiaxed Transition in Laser Welding: A Phase-Field Study
process_methodology: Quantitative 2D Phase-Field Model with Karma thin-interface asymptotics and auxiliary anti-trapping current; Explicit finite difference solver; Solute conservation and constitutional supercooling analysis.

observations:
• Investigated the dynamic solutal interactions between advancing columnar dendritic fronts and nucleating equiaxed grains.

• Competitive growth between adjacent equiaxed grains leads to solutal impingement and secondary arm coarsening.
results:
• Phase-field maps clearly show the solutal blocking mechanism: equiaxed solute halos physically engulf and halt columnar dendrite tips.
• Columnar dendrites exhibit tip splitting and lateral branching when encountering the asymmetric solutal field of equiaxed grains.

my_comments:

title: Residual Stress Formation and Control in Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing: Mechanisms, Characterization, and Mitigation Strategies
journal: Journal of Mechanical Science and Technology, 40(9):6663–6685
material: Comprehensive Review (Structural Steels, Titanium, Aluminum, Inconel Superalloys)
process_methodology: Comprehensive critical review; Residual stress origin mechanics (thermal contraction, solid-state phase transformation, structural constraint); Measurement methods (neutron diffraction, synchrotron XRD, contour method, hole drilling, DIC); In-situ and ex-situ mitigation taxonomy.
key_params: In-situ rolling forces: 50–100 kN; Ultrasonic impact frequencies: 20–30 kHz; Substrate preheating: 100–400°C; Trailing thermoelectric cooling: 10–50°C/s; Post-weld heat treatment (PWHT).
observations:
• Residual stress in WAAM is primarily thermal-contraction driven, resulting in high longitudinal tensile stress along the deposition path.
• Peak tensile residual stresses consistently concentrate at the top deposited surface and the deposit-substrate interface boundary.
• In austenitic stainless steels, titanium, and nickel alloys, tensile residual stress frequently reaches 80–100% of room-temperature yield strength.
• In ferritic and martensitic steels, volumetric expansion during solid-state phase transformation counteracts thermal contraction, lowering peak stresses.
• In-situ high-pressure interpass rolling (50–100 kN) induces deep compressive plastic deformation, converting tensile stresses to compression.
• Interpass cooling and optimized clamping reduce global distortion by up to 40% but can elevate localized internal residual stress.
results:
• Longitudinal residual stress profiles in non-transforming alloys show monolithic tensile peaks, whereas transforming steels show M-shaped valleys.
• Interpass rolling and ultrasonic impact peening create a deep compressive surface barrier that inhibits fatigue crack initiation.
• In-situ rolling reduces residual stress peaks by up to 75% and completely suppresses component distortion.
• Trailing thermoelectric cooling reduces baseline thermal accumulation and cuts distortion by 40%.
• Post-weld stress-relief heat treatment relieves 70–90% of accumulated residual stresses across Ti-6Al-4V and steel builds.
future_work:
• Developing fast, non-destructive in-situ residual stress measurement techniques suitable for live monitoring during deposition.
• Formulating unified fracture mechanics models to predict fatigue crack growth in the presence of complex multiaxial residual stress fields.
my_comments:
• Essential comprehensive literature review on residual stress mechanics in WAAM.
• Distinguishes between global distortion mitigation (clamping/cooling) and internal stress relief (rolling/peening/PWHT).

title: Modelling of Wire-Arc Additive Manufacturing – A Review

title: Development of Multi-Material Components via Robotic Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing
journal: International Journal of 3D Printing Technologies and Digital Industry, 5(3):721–729
material: ER70S-6 (Ferritic Low Carbon Steel) + ER316L (Austenitic Stainless Steel)
process_methodology: Robotic GMAW-WAAM (Gedik Welding / Motoman robot); Sequential deposition of 10 layers ER70S-6 base followed by 10 layers ER316L top; Optical microscopy, SEM, EDS elemental area/line mapping; High-density Vickers microhardness (HV5) profiling.

observations:
• Successfully manufactured a defect-free, fully dense bimetallic component joining low-carbon steel (ER70S-6) and stainless steel (ER316L).

• Carbon diffusion creates a distinct carbon-depleted, soft heat-affected zone (HAZ) on the ferritic side of the fusion boundary.
• The stainless steel interface boundary becomes carbon-enriched, promoting localized martensitic/bainitic hardening upon rapid cooling.
• Microstructure displays strong epitaxial grain growth on the ferritic side transitioning to cellular-dendritic austenite with skeletal delta-ferrite.
results:
• EDS elemental line scans confirm smooth, continuous diffusion gradients of Cr, Ni, and Fe across the 100 μm wide transition zone.

my_comments:

title: Recent Progress and Scientific Challenges in Wire-Arc Additive Manufacturing of Metallic Multi-Material Structures
journal: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing, 9(8):284
material: Multi-Material Systems (Steel-Stainless Steel, Steel-Nickel, Ti-Al, Fe-Al, Cu-Steel FGMs)
process_methodology: Comprehensive state-of-the-art review covering 160+ publications; Metallurgical compatibility criteria (Hume-Rothery, formation enthalpy ΔH_mix, CTE mismatch Δα); Interfacial intermetallic compound (IMC) kinetics; Defect mitigation strategies.
key_params: Arc modes: CMT, Pulsed GMAW, Tandem Wire, Plasma-TIG; Heat inputs: 0.2–1.8 kJ/mm; Interpass temperatures: 50–250°C; Deposition rates: 2–10 kg/h; Intermediate buffer interlayers (Ni, V, Cu, Cr).
observations:
• Multi-material WAAM offers massive deposition rate advantages (2–10 kg/h) and cost efficiency for large multi-metal parts compared to powder AM.
• Identified three core scientific bottlenecks: (1) brittle interfacial IMC formation, (2) thermal expansion mismatch cracking, and (3) solute macrosegregation.
• Direct joining of highly dissimilar pairs (e.g. Ti-Al, Fe-Al) forms continuous brittle intermetallic layers (FeAl3, Fe3Al, TiAl3, NiTi2) that crack spontaneously.
• Thermal expansion mismatch (Δα > 5×10^-6 /K) induces severe interfacial shear residual stresses during cooling.
• Designing intermediate functionally graded transition layers or compatible buffer metals (e.g. Ti-V-Cr-Fe or Cu-Ni-Steel) eliminates brittle IMCs.
• Active thermal control (low heat input CMT mode, interpass cooling, ultrasonic assistance) suppresses excessive liquid-state interdiffusion.
results:
• Interlayer buffering transforms continuous brittle intermetallic films into isolated, harmless dispersed precipitates.
• Microstructural transitions across graded zones show smooth crystallographic lattice parameter adaptation without micro-fissuring.
• Properly designed functionally graded buffer layers recover joint tensile efficiency up to 85–95% of the weaker parent metal (vs. <30% for unbuffered joints).
• Thermal expansion mismatch Δα > 25% increases interfacial cracking susceptibility by over 70%.
• CMT arc control restricts the interfacial IMC layer thickness below the critical 2–5 μm brittleness threshold.
future_work:
• Developing dynamic CALPHAD-coupled CFD models to predict non-equilibrium phase formation in dissimilar melt pools.
• Establishing standardized fatigue, creep, and fracture toughness design codes for additively manufactured multi-materials.
my_comments:
• Definitive modern review on multi-material WAAM thermodynamics and interfacial mechanics.
• Essential guide for selecting buffer metals and predicting brittle intermetallic reactions.

title: Wire-Based Additive Manufacturing of Multi-Material Structures: A Review

key_params: Technology share: WAAM accounts for 70–80% of wire AM; Deposition rates: WAAM (2–10 kg/h) vs. LWAM (0.5–2 kg/h) vs. EBAM (1–5 kg/h); Heat inputs: 0.15–2.0 kJ/mm; Material utilization: ~95%.

future_work:

• 3D multi-component phase-field simulations to model complex multi-phase microstructures in graded wire deposition.
my_comments:
• Excellent technological comparison between WAAM, Laser-Wire, and Electron Beam wire AM.
• Confirms WAAM's dominance (70–80% share) for large-scale multi-material components.

title: Phase Field Modeling of Dendritic Growth and Coarsening in Al-Si Binary Alloys
process_methodology: 2D Phase-Field Model based on Kim-Kim-Suzuki (KKS) framework coupled with solute diffusion and thermal fields; Explicit Finite Difference Method (FDM) on regular Cartesian grid; Anisotropic interfacial energy.
key_params: Liquidus slope m = -6.6 K/wt%; Partition coefficient k0 = 0.13; Melting point Tm = 933.4 K; Gibbs-Thomson coefficient Γ = 1.96×10^-7 K·m; Grid spacing Δx = 0.03 μm; Time step Δt = 1.0×10^-7 s; 4-fold anisotropy ε4 = 0.01–0.05.
observations:
• Formulated a quantitative diffuse-interface model for binary alloy solidification based on the KKS free energy framework.
• Incorporated 4-fold anisotropic interfacial energy σ(θ) = σ0[1 + ε4·cos(4θ)] to drive preferred <100> dendritic growth.
• Simulated steady-state primary dendritic tip velocity, tip radius selection, and secondary side-branching dynamics.
• Demonstrated that side-branching is triggered by thermal/solutal noise perturbations and competitive arm growth.
• Investigated isothermal coarsening (Ostwald ripening) of secondary dendrite arms driven by capillary curvature differences.
• Smaller secondary arms with higher mean curvature dissolve, transferring solute to thicker primary trunks over time.
results:
• Phase-field simulations capture the complete morphological evolution from initial spherical seed to 4-fold branched dendrite.
• Ostwald ripening simulations show remelting of necked side-arms and coalescence of adjacent dendritic arms.
• Steady-state dendritic tip velocity scales with undercooling as V_tip ∝ ΔT^2.6, validating Ivantsov transport theory.
• Secondary Dendrite Arm Spacing (SDAS) coarsening exponent verified at n ≈ 0.32–0.34 (matching theoretical LSW t^1/3 law).
• Solute concentration at the dendrite core accurately matches k0·C0 without unphysical solute trapping.
future_work:
