• Incorporating fluid convection (melt flow) to investigate the effect of flow shearing on side-arm detachments.
my_comments:
• Clear, pedagogical phase-field formulation for binary alloy solidification and coarsening.
• Excellent benchmark for validating dendritic tip kinematics and Ostwald ripening scaling in Al alloys.

title: Modeling Melt Convection in Phase-Field Simulations of Solidification
process_methodology: Unified diffuse-interface model coupling Phase-Field equations with Navier-Stokes momentum equations; Interfacial dissipative drag resistivity formulation; Finite Volume / Finite Difference discretization; Thin-interface asymptotic analysis.
key_params: Interface thickness W0; Kinematic viscosity ν; Prandtl number Pr = 1.0; Reynolds number Re = 0.1–10; Péclet number Pe = 0.1–5.0; Interfacial drag function h(φ) = φ² / (1-φ)³ (Carman-Kozeny porous media law).
observations:
• Formulated a revolutionary diffuse-interface framework where Navier-Stokes equations are coupled to phase-field equations across diffuse boundaries.
• Interfacial drag resistivity term naturally enforces the no-slip boundary condition at the solid-liquid interface without front tracking.
• Melt convection upstream compresses the thermal and solutal boundary layers, steepening gradients at the advancing dendritic tip.
• Upstream dendritic tip growth velocity is dramatically accelerated while tip radius sharpens.
• Downstream dendritic growth is severely retarded or completely arrested due to the warm, solute-enriched flow wash.
• Convective flow induces asymmetric secondary side-branching preferentially on the upstream flanks and tilts dendritic growth toward the flow.
results:
• Fluid streamline contours show smooth deflection around complex dendritic geometries with zero-velocity enforced inside the solid phase.
• Morphological asymmetry: upstream arms grow robustly while downstream arms undergo complete stunting and dissolution.
• Upstream dendritic tip velocity increases by 200% to 400% under forced flow (Pe > 1) compared to stagnant melt growth.
• Dendritic tip radius R_tip decreases by ~35% on the upstream side.
• Diffuse-interface drag formulation recovers analytical sharp-interface fluid velocity profiles within O(ε) error.
future_work:
• Extending the coupled Phase-Field Navier-Stokes model to multi-component alloys with strong thermo-solutal buoyancy convection.
• Implementing adaptive octree meshing to handle 3D convective dendritic growth at high Reynolds numbers.
my_comments:
• The seminal, highly-cited cornerstone paper for coupling fluid flow with phase-field solidification.
• The Carman-Kozeny drag formulation is the universal standard for enforcing no-slip in diffuse interface models.

title: Phase-Field Formulation for Quantitative Modeling of Alloy Solidification
material: Binary Alloys (Model Solute System / Vanishing Solid Diffusivity)
process_methodology: Thin-interface asymptotic analysis of the phase-field equations carried to second order in interface width W0; Introduction of the auxiliary solute anti-trapping current j_at; Elimination of artificial interface kinetics and non-equilibrium solute trapping.
key_params: Anti-trapping current coefficient a_at = 1/(2√2); Interface width W0 / d0 ~ 10–100; Chemical potential formulation u; Vanishing solid diffusivity Ds → 0; Capillary length d0; Solute partition coefficient k.
observations:
• Solved the fundamental limitation of phase-field models requiring atomic-scale grid resolution to simulate alloy solidification.
• Standard diffuse-interface models exhibit artificial solute trapping and interface stretching kinetics when interface width W0 exceeds physical width.
• Formulated an auxiliary solute anti-trapping current j_at = -a_at·W0·(1-k)·(∂φ/∂t)·(∇φ / |∇φ|) added to the solute conservation equation.
• Anti-trapping flux precisely cancels out the non-physical solute accumulation caused by the finite thickness of the diffuse interface.
• Thin-interface asymptotics rigorously map phase-field parameters to macroscopic Gibbs-Thomson relation and solute conservation conditions.
• Enables quantitative, grid-independent simulations of dendritic growth at experimentally realistic low supercoolings (Δ ≪ 1).
results:
• Completely eliminates spurious solute trapping across the diffuse boundary, enabling accurate simulation with Ds = 0 in the solid.
• Dendritic tip operating state perfectly obeys microscopic solvability theory without numerical grid-pinning artifacts.
• Predicted dendritic tip velocity V and selection parameter σ* = 2·D_L·d0 / (R²·V) ≈ 0.017 match solvability theory within <2%.
• Convergence is verified across interface widths varying over an order of magnitude (W0/d0 = 10 to 80).
• 1D planar partition profiles match exact Scheil and analytical sharp-interface solutions.
future_work:
• Formulating multi-component anti-trapping current tensors for ternary and multi-component commercial superalloys.
• Coupling the thin-interface formulation with high-performance GPU-accelerated AMR solvers.
my_comments:
• The single most important theoretical breakthrough in quantitative phase-field modeling of alloy solidification.
• Mandatory foundation for any quantitative solidification simulation in the Master's thesis.

title: Phase-Field Model for Binary Alloys (The KKS Model)
process_methodology: Free-energy-based Phase-Field Model with equal chemical potential constraint (KKS Model); Definition of local concentration as c = h(φ)·cs + [1-h(φ)]·cl; Matched asymptotic expansions; 1D and 2D finite difference simulations.
key_params: Interfacial energy σ; Interface width 2λ; Gradient energy coefficient ε² = (3/2)·σ·λ; Barrier height w = 6σ/λ; Chemical potential constraint: μs(cs) = μl(cl) = μ; Solid/liquid partition coefficient k.
observations:
• Developed the world-renowned Kim-Kim-Suzuki (KKS) model, resolving the thermodynamic inconsistency of the earlier WBM model.
• In the KKS model, the interfacial region is treated as a mixture of solid and liquid phases with distinct local concentrations cs and cl.
• Enforced an equal chemical potential constraint (μs(cs) = μl(cl)) at every point within the diffuse interface.
• Eliminates the unphysical excess interfacial free energy and artificial solute adsorption present in the WBM formulation.
• Allows the phase-field interface width 2λ to be chosen arbitrarily large (up to 50× physical width) without modifying bulk thermodynamics.
• Establishes direct mathematical relationships between phase-field parameters (ε, w, M) and physical properties (σ, Tm, m, k, D_L).
results:
• 1D solute concentration profiles show smooth, monotonic transitions across the interface without unphysical solute spikes.
• 2D dendritic simulations accurately capture parabolic tip geometry and secondary arm branching dynamics.
• Phase diagram equilibrium compositions at flat interfaces are recovered with zero thermodynamic error.
• 1D planar front steady-state solute redistribution matches exact sharp-interface analytical solutions across wide growth rates.
• Interface width can be chosen up to 50× larger than physical width without altering interfacial driving forces.
future_work:
• Extending the KKS equal chemical potential formulation to multi-phase, multi-component systems coupled with CALPHAD databases.
• Developing accelerated non-linear iterative root-finding algorithms for solving local chemical potential constraints on massive parallel grids.
my_comments:
• The definitive thermodynamic phase-field model (KKS) implemented in major codes like MICRESS, PACE3D, and MOOSE.
• Understanding the equal chemical potential constraint is essential for thesis PFM derivations.

title: Phase-Field Simulations of Non-Isothermal Binary Alloy Solidification
process_methodology: Coupled non-isothermal Phase-Field, energy conservation (with latent heat source L·∂φ/∂t), and solute diffusion equations; Adaptive Finite Element Method (FEM) on unstructured triangular meshes; Solute and thermal boundary conditions.
key_params: Ni-Cu alloy (C0 = 0.408 Cu); Latent heat L = 2.35×10^9 J/m³; Thermal diffusivity α = 1.0×10^-5 m²/s; Solute diffusivity D_L = 1.0×10^-9 m²/s; Lewis number Le = α/D_L ~ 10^4; Anisotropy δ = 0.02–0.04; Prescribed cooling vs. constant heat extraction.
observations:
• Formulated a coupled non-isothermal phase-field model that simultaneously accounts for solute redistribution and latent heat generation.
• Solved the governing equations using an adaptive unstructured finite element method, dynamically refining elements near the moving interface.
• Latent heat released at the advancing solidification front elevates local temperature, creating a localized thermal boundary layer.
• Local thermal buildup lowers effective undercooling, retarding primary dendritic tip velocity compared to isothermal assumptions.
• Under constant heat extraction conditions, recalescence occurs where interface temperature rebounds toward the liquidus.
• Recalescence slows primary tip advance, allowing secondary side-branches to thicken and undergo competitive coarsening.
results:
• Adaptive triangular mesh dynamically clusters around the solid-liquid interface, maintaining high resolution with minimal DOFs.
• Thermal contours show localized heating around the dendritic tip which broadens the thermal envelope into the melt.
• In non-isothermal growth, dendritic tip radius R_tip increases by 15% to 30% compared to pure isothermal conditions.
• Primary tip velocity V_tip decreases by 20% to 50% due to local latent heat rejection.
• Adaptive mesh refinement achieves identical numerical accuracy with 85% fewer degrees of freedom than uniform grids.
future_work:
• Extending the non-isothermal adaptive FEM model to 3D domains to capture multi-directional heat dissipation.
• Incorporating fluid convection to investigate how melt flow sweeps away rejected latent heat from the dendritic tip.
my_comments:
• Demonstrates why non-isothermal modeling is critical: latent heat rejection significantly alters dendritic tip kinematics.
• The Lewis number Le ~ 10^4 highlights the massive disparity between thermal and solutal diffusion lengths.

title: Phase-Field Model for Non-Isothermal Phase Transitions in Binary Alloys (WBM-II Model)
process_methodology: Thermodynamically consistent Phase-Field formulation derived from a global entropy functional S(e, c, φ); Variational derivatives coupled with Onsager phenomenological coefficients; Asymptotic analysis to sharp-interface limits.
key_params: Entropy density functional S; Internal energy e; Solute concentration c; Order parameter φ; Gradient energy coefficients ε_e, ε_c, ε_φ; Positive-definite Onsager mobility matrix; Non-negative local entropy production S_gen ≥ 0.
observations:
• Developed a fully thermodynamically consistent phase-field model for non-isothermal solidification derived from an entropy functional.
• Ensures that the local rate of entropy production is strictly non-negative (S_gen ≥ 0), rigorously satisfying the Second Law of Thermodynamics.
• Governing equations for phase field φ, solute concentration c, and internal energy e arise naturally from variational principles.
• Demonstrates that solute trapping and non-equilibrium partition coefficients emerge naturally as kinetic limits at high interface velocities.
• Matched asymptotic expansions prove that the diffuse interface converges exactly to classical energy and solute conservation conditions.
• Establishes the mathematical framework for multi-field (thermal + solutal + structural) phase-field coupling.
results:
• Formulated the fundamental entropy-gradient thermodynamic potential for non-isothermal alloy phase transitions.
• Proves that diffuse-interface kinetic laws naturally recover sharp-interface Stefan and Gibbs-Thomson relations.
• Matches classical sharp-interface energy conservation KS·(∂TS/∂n) - KL·(∂TL/∂n) = L·Vn in the asymptotic limit ε_φ → 0.
• Captures solute trapping kinetics where the effective partition coefficient k(V) transitions from k0 to 1 as V → D_i / W.
• Validated 1D planar solidification stability and recalescence temperature profiles under rapid cooling.
future_work:
• Combining the entropy-functional thermodynamic consistency with the KKS equal chemical potential model.
• Applying the non-isothermal formulation to rapid solidification conditions typical of laser and electron beam additive manufacturing.
my_comments:
• Landmark theoretical paper proving thermodynamic consistency (2nd Law) in non-isothermal phase-field models.
• Elegant variational derivation connecting entropy functionals with Onsager reciprocity.

title: Phase-Field Simulation for Non-Isothermal Solidification of Al-Cu Binary Alloy
process_methodology: Coupled non-isothermal Phase-Field, concentration, and temperature equations; Dilute solution thermodynamic approximation; 2D Finite Difference Method (FDM); Investigation of thermal undercooling, noise perturbation, and anisotropy.
key_params: Al-4.5% Cu; Liquidus slope m = -3.44 K/wt%; Partition coeff k0 = 0.17; Melting point Tm = 933.6 K; Gibbs-Thomson coeff Γ = 2.41×10^-7 K·m; Grid: 300×300; Δx = 0.03 μm; Δt = 2.0×10^-8 s; Undercooling ΔT = 10–30 K; Anisotropy ε = 0.02.
observations:
• Simulated free dendritic growth of Al-4.5 wt% Cu alloy under non-isothermal conditions with varying undercooling and anisotropy.
• Higher thermal undercooling accelerates primary dendritic tip growth velocity and narrows the dendritic trunk width.
• Anisotropic interfacial energy strength (ε > 0.03) sharpens dendritic tips, promotes <100> crystallographic alignment, and suppresses tip splitting.
• Random thermal perturbations trigger secondary side-branching along the primary dendritic trunk flanks.
• Secondary arms compete for rejected copper solute; only arms with sufficient inter-branch diffusion space survive and coarsen.
• Copper solute strongly segregates into the inter-dendritic liquid channels, reaching terminal eutectic concentrations.
results:
• 2D concentration maps reveal severe copper microsegregation with solute-enriched liquid films surrounding dendrite arms.
• Strong 4-fold anisotropy produces well-defined orthogonal dendritic crosses, while low anisotropy causes degenerate tip splitting.
• Dendritic tip velocity scales linearly with undercooling: V_tip ≈ 0.012 m/s at ΔT = 10 K to 0.048 m/s at ΔT = 30 K.
• Inter-dendritic copper concentration in the terminal liquid reached 18.0 wt% Cu (meeting the eutectic θ-Al2Cu formation threshold).
• Secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) decreased from 1.8 μm to 0.7 μm as undercooling increased from 10 K to 30 K.
future_work:
• Incorporating solid-state back-diffusion during post-solidification cooling to evaluate homogenization of Cu coring.
• 3D simulations coupling thermal stress to predict localized solidification cracking along solute-enriched inter-dendritic liquid films.
my_comments:
• Provides direct quantitative parameters and microsegregation contours for Al-Cu alloys.
• Solute buildup to 18 wt% Cu explains why 2xxx series aluminum is highly prone to hot tearing during welding.

title: Phase-Field Simulation of Solidification
material: Comprehensive Review of Pure Metals, Binary/Ternary Alloys, Eutectic & Peritectic Systems
process_methodology: Authoritative review of Phase-Field Modeling for solidification; Mathematical structure of diffuse interfaces; Asymptotic analysis (classical, thin-interface); Thermodynamics of free energy functionals; Discretization and multiscale coupling methods.
key_params: Order parameters: scalar phase field φ, vector/quaternion grain orientations η_i; Non-dimensional numbers: Péclet Pe, Lewis Le, Stefan St, Reynolds Re; Anisotropy functions; Thin-interface asymptotics.
observations:
• Comprehensive review synthesizing the emergence of phase-field models as the dominant computational tool in solidification science.
• Phase-field methods eliminate the need to explicitly track complex, moving solid-liquid topological boundaries in 2D and 3D.
• Categorized models into classical sharp-interface asymptotics, KKS chemical potential models, and Karma thin-interface asymptotics.
• Highlights the ability of phase-field models to simulate complex microstructure topologies: dendritic, cellular, eutectic, and peritectic.
• Multi-phase-field models successfully simulate polycrystalline grain competition, grain boundary groove angles, and CET.
• Identifies computational efficiency and multiscale coupling with macro-thermal models as the primary frontier for industrial applications.
results:
• Demonstrates universal phase-field capabilities across pure dendrites, regular lamellar eutectics, and peritectic envelope growth.
• Reviews thin-interface formulations that eliminate artificial interface kinetics without atomic-scale grid constraints.
• Validates phase-field dendritic tip velocity and tip radius selection against Ivantsov and solvability theory with <1% error.
• Eutectic lamellar spacing predictions match the classical Jackson-Hunt scaling relation (λ²·V = const).
• Directional solidification cellular-to-dendritic transition velocities accurately reproduce Mullins-Sekerka stability thresholds.
future_work:
• Developing accelerated adaptive multi-grid and GPU-parallel solvers for meter-scale 3D engineering components.
• Direct thermodynamic and kinetic database coupling (CALPHAD) for multi-component commercial alloys.
my_comments:
• The definitive, authoritative review on phase-field modeling of solidification.
• Mandatory core citation providing the theoretical foundation for the entire thesis modeling chapter.

title: Phase-Field Model of Dendritic Growth in Binary and Ternary Alloys
material: Fe-C, Fe-P, Fe-C-P Ternary Steels & Al-Cu Alloys
process_methodology: Thin-interface Phase-Field model extended to ternary dilute alloys based on KKS equal chemical potential formulation; 2D explicit Finite Difference Method; Secondary Dendrite Arm Spacing (SDAS, λ2) prediction.
key_params: Fe-C (m_C = -78.0 K/wt%, k_C = 0.17); Fe-P (m_P = -31.3 K/wt%, k_P = 0.06); Al-Cu (m_Cu = -3.4 K/wt%, k_Cu = 0.14); Interface mobility M; Solidification time t_f; Cooling rate R_c = 1–100 K/s.
observations:
• Extended the quantitative KKS phase-field formulation to ternary dilute alloys (Fe-C-P) at the thin-interface limit.
• Evaluated the coupled redistribution of both fast-diffusing interstitial carbon and slow-diffusing substitutional phosphorus.
• Addition of phosphorus significantly increases the total constitutional undercooling ahead of the advancing dendritic tip.
• Enhanced constitutional undercooling sharpens the primary dendritic tip radius and accelerates tip growth velocity.
• Evaluated the evolution of Secondary Dendrite Arm Spacing (SDAS, λ2) as a function of cooling rate and local solidification time t_f.
• Demonstrated that phase-field simulations naturally capture the power-law kinetics of secondary arm coarsening.
results:
• Phase-field simulations reveal complex ternary solute interactions: phosphorus strongly segregates into inter-dendritic spaces.
• Secondary dendrite arm morphology exhibits competitive coarsening with larger arms consuming smaller neighbors.
• Secondary Dendrite Arm Spacing follows the power law λ2 = A·(t_f)^n with coarsening exponent n = 0.33±0.02 for both Fe-C and Al-Cu.
• Power-law exponent n = 0.33 perfectly validates the classical Kattamis-Coughlin coarsening theory.
• Phosphorus exhibits severe microsegregation (reaching 4.5× nominal composition in liquid) due to its low partition coefficient (k_P = 0.06).
future_work:
• Incorporating off-diagonal cross-diffusion terms (Onsager diffusion matrix) between carbon and alloying elements in the liquid phase.
• Extending to multi-component stainless steels (Fe-Cr-Ni-Mo-C) for direct application to WAAM microstructures.
my_comments:
• Essential reference for multi-component dendritic solidification.
• Proves that phase-field simulations quantitatively reproduce the experimental SDAS scaling law (λ2 ∝ t_f^1/3).

title: The Phase-Field Method: Simulation of Alloy Dendritic Solidification during Recalescence
process_methodology: Coupled non-isothermal Phase-Field, solute diffusion, and heat conservation equations (WBM formulation); 2D explicit time-stepping Finite Difference Method on uniform Cartesian mesh; High initial undercooling and recalescence analysis.
key_params: Ni-Cu alloy (C0 = 0.408 Cu); Hypercooling limit ΔT_hyp = L/Cp ≈ 400 K; Grid: 400×400 to 600×600; Interface thickness parameter ε; High initial thermal supercooling.
observations:
• Investigated dendritic growth of a binary alloy into a highly undercooled melt undergoing rapid recalescence.
• Solved coupled equations for order parameter φ, solute concentration c, and temperature T on uniform Cartesian grids.
• At early stages (high undercooling), dendritic growth is governed by rapid thermal diffusion with significant solute trapping.
• As latent heat is released, the surrounding melt warms rapidly (recalescence), raising interface temperature back toward the liquidus.
• Onset of recalescence causes a dramatic slowdown in primary dendritic tip velocity by over an order of magnitude.
• Solidification shifts from thermally controlled growth to solute-diffusion-limited growth, triggering intense secondary arm proliferation.
results:
• Captures the transition from smooth needle-like thermal dendrites to highly branched solutal dendrites during recalescence.
• 2D concentration contours accurately reproduce core-to-rim microsegregation (coring) profiles across dendrite trunks.
• Captured the full recalescence temperature-time history ΔT(t), showing rapid thermal rebound within microseconds.
• Primary tip velocity drops by >90% upon the onset of recalescence as thermal undercooling collapses.
• Solute concentration at the dendrite core reflects non-equilibrium solute trapping at high initial velocities.
future_work:
• Reformulating the recalescence model using Karma thin-interface asymptotics to eliminate finite-interface solute adsorption.
• Simulating cyclic recalescence during rapid multi-track additive manufacturing thermal pulses.
my_comments:
• Classic, fundamental paper explaining the physics of recalescence during rapid solidification.
• Clearly illustrates the transition from thermal-driven growth to solute-diffusion-controlled dendritic branching.

title: Prediction of Dendritic Growth and Microsegregation Patterns in a Binary Alloy Using the Phase-Field Method
process_methodology: Isothermal Phase-Field Model for binary alloy solidification (WBM formulation); Regular solution thermodynamics; 2D Finite Difference Method on uniform Cartesian grids; Systematic variation of undercooling and 4-fold anisotropy.
key_params: Dimensionless undercooling Δ = (TL - T)/(TL - TS); 4-fold anisotropy ε4 = 0.01–0.04; Interfacial energy σ0; Grid size Δx = 0.005 dimensionless units; Ideal solution free energy parameters.
observations:
• First historic paper to demonstrate quantitative 2D microsegregation maps predicted directly from phase-field simulations.
• Treated bulk liquid and solid phases as regular solutions with a diffuse order parameter describing interfacial transitions.
• Evaluated the dependence of primary tip velocity, tip radius, and side-branching frequency on undercooling and anisotropy.
• Confirmed that phase-field predictions of steady-state tip operating state (V·R² = const) match classical LKT marginal stability theory.
• Side-branches initiate spontaneously through the amplification of numerical and thermal noise perturbations.
• Successfully reproduced dendritic coring profiles and solute buildup in inter-dendritic liquid pools without empirical assumptions.
results:
• Generated the first comprehensive 2D phase-field maps showing dendritic morphology, side-arm branching, and microsegregation.
• Demonstrated that 4-fold anisotropy is mandatory to maintain stable dendritic tip growth and prevent tip splitting.
• Dendritic tip selection parameter σ* = 2·D_L·d0 / (R²·V) ≈ 0.02 validated across various undercoolings against marginal stability theory.
• Solute concentration in the primary dendrite core matches equilibrium k0·C0 at low undercoolings.
• Side-branch spacing decreased systematically with increasing undercooling.
future_work:
• Incorporating non-isothermal thermal fields and latent heat transport.
• Developing adaptive mesh algorithms to overcome the extreme computational memory cost of 2D/3D uniform Cartesian grids.
my_comments:
• Historic foundation for predicting microsegregation and dendritic coring using phase-field methods.
• Paved the way for modern quantitative microstructural simulations in welding and additive manufacturing.

title: Phase-Field Model for Isothermal Phase Transitions in Binary Alloys (The WBM-I Model)
process_methodology: Foundational Ginzburg-Landau gradient energy phase-field derivation; Coupling of Cahn-Hilliard equation for conserved solute c and Allen-Cahn equation for non-conserved order parameter φ; Asymptotic analysis to sharp-interface Stefan problem; 1D and 2D finite difference.
key_params: Free energy functional F = ∫ [f(c,φ) + (1/2)·ε²·|∇φ|²] dV; Double-well potential g(φ) = φ²·(1-φ)²; Interpolation function p(φ) = φ³·(10 - 15φ + 6φ²); Gradient energy coefficient ε; Interfacial mobility M.
observations:
• The landmark seminal paper that birthed the entire field of phase-field modeling for alloy solidification (WBM-I model).
• Formulated a diffuse-interface model for binary alloys based on gradient thermodynamics and Ginzburg-Landau free energy functionals.
• Coupled the Cahn-Hilliard diffusion equation for conserved solute concentration with the Allen-Cahn equation for phase order parameter.
• Proved mathematically that diffuse-interface governing equations converge to the classical sharp-interface Stefan problem as ε → 0.
• Diffuse-interface formulation naturally incorporates surface tension (Gibbs-Thomson effect), interface kinetics, and solute rejection without front tracking.
• Simulated 1D planar front stability, Mullins-Sekerka morphological instability, and 2D cellular solidification transitions.
results:
• Established the standard mathematical formulation for alloy phase-field modeling used across materials science.
• Successfully simulated the morphological transition from stable planar interface to cellular/dendritic fingers.
• Proved exact mathematical convergence of the diffuse interface to the classical Gibbs-Thomson relation: T_int = Tm + m·c_L - Γ·κ - V/μ_k.
• Demonstrated 1D planar front solute segregation profiles matching sharp-interface analytical solutions.
• Established mathematical relationships between gradient coefficient ε, barrier height w, and physical surface energy σ.
future_work:
• Developing thin-interface formulations (achieved by Karma in 2001) to eliminate excess interface solute adsorption at finite ε.
• Extending to multi-component, multi-phase systems with non-ideal thermodynamic databases.
my_comments:
• The monumental foundational paper of phase-field solidification modeling (Wheeler-Boettinger-McFadden 1992).
• Essential historical citation establishing the origin of gradient energy diffuse-interface methods.

title: Ultrasonically Assisted Hot-Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing Process of AA7075 Metal Matrix Nanocomposite
material: AA7075 Metal Matrix Nanocomposite (AA7075 + 1.7 vol% TiB2 nanoparticles)
process_methodology: Ultrasonically assisted hot-wire gas tungsten arc additive manufacturing (UA-HWAAM); Resistance pre-heating of TiB2/AA7075 feedstock wire coupled with immersed ultrasonic probe (20 kHz, 0–60% amplitude) directly behind the GTA arc pool; In-situ FLIR IR thermal imaging; Micro-tensile DIC testing and Vickers hardness mapping.
key_params: Wire diameter: 1.2 mm (AA7075 + 1.7 vol% TiB2); Current: 65–80 A, Voltage: 10 V (heat input reduced layer-by-layer: 80A L1 -> 75A L2 -> 70A L3 -> 65A L4+); Hot-wire resistance current: ~40 A; Travel speed: 2 ipm (0.85 mm/s) vs 3 ipm (1.27 mm/s); Wire feed speed: 20–30 ipm; Ultrasonic frequency: 20 kHz; UA power amplitude: 0%, 30%, 60%; Melt pool peak temp: ~1359 °C (2 ipm) vs 1270 °C (3 ipm); Argon shield gas: 25 CFH (11.8 L/min).
observations:
• Hot-wire resistance heating preheats the wire, cleaning wire surface contaminants and significantly increasing deposition rate compared to cold-wire GTA-WAAM.
• Direct immersion of the ultrasonic probe behind the arc eliminates acoustic energy attenuation typically observed in substrate-vibration setups.
• Immersed ultrasonic probe applies intermolecular adhesive constraint at the melt pool top surface, generating a characteristic steeple-roof bead geometry and preventing melt run-off.
• Acoustic cavitation and high-intensity acoustic streaming disperse agglomerated TiB2 nanoparticles uniformly throughout the matrix melt pool.
• TiB2 nanoparticles act as heterogeneous nucleation sites, which, coupled with ultrasonic dendrite fragmentation, promotes a fine, uniform equiaxed grain structure across both interlayer and bulk regions.
• High-intensity acoustic streaming accelerates the flotation and escape of hydrogen gas bubbles, suppressing microporosity formation.
• Lower torch travel speed (2 ipm vs 3 ipm) prolongs the ultrasonic-melt interaction time, maximizing the de-agglomeration and degasification efficiency.
results:
• Synergistic integration of hot-wire preheating and acoustic cavitation reduced internal porosity from 1.82% in conventional WAAM down to below 0.12% in UA-HWAAM.
• Acoustic streaming and shockwaves broke up 40–60 nm TiB2 nanoparticle clusters, eliminating particle-depleted zones and achieving a homogeneous nano-reinforcement distribution.
• Cross-sectional Vickers microhardness improved from 115 ± 8 HV in conventional deposits to 148 ± 5 HV in UA-HWAAM, with a highly uniform hardness profile across layer boundaries.
• In-situ DIC micro-tensile evaluation demonstrated an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 468 ± 12 MPa and yield strength (YS) of 342 ± 9 MPa with 7.4% elongation in UA-HWAAM (2 ipm, 30% UA), outperforming conventional WAAM by over 28% in strength.
• The steeple-roof surface profile generated by probe meniscus forces enhanced vertical build height per pass from 0.84 mm to 2.10 mm without triggering edge collapse or lack-of-fusion defects.
future_work:
• Multi-physics phase-field modeling of nanoparticle pushing and engulfment dynamics under acoustic streaming flows in complex 7xxx alloys.
• Investigation of post-deposition T6 solution and artificial aging heat treatment schedules to optimize η' (MgZn2) precipitation strengthening alongside TiB2 dispersoids.
• Closed-loop acoustic power and torch travel speed control to dynamically regulate melt pool geometry and thermal gradients during large-scale component builds.
my_comments:
• Masterfully addresses two fundamental bottlenecks of 7xxx WAAM: solidification cracking (via TiB2 inoculation) and high porosity/low deposition rate (via hot-wire + immersed ultrasonic cavitation).
• Immersed ultrasonic probe method is vastly superior to substrate sonication for tall builds since acoustic energy does not attenuate with increasing build height.

title: A Long-Term and Pragmatic Numerical Simulation of Wire Arc Additively Manufactured ER70S6 and ER316L Thin-Wall via Finite Difference Method
material: ER70S-6 Low Carbon Steel and ER316L Austenitic Stainless Steel
process_methodology: 3D Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) model based on the Finite Difference Method (FDM) coupled with Volume of Fluid (VOF) free-surface tracking; Navier-Stokes momentum equations with Carman-Kozeny porous media drag; Enthalpy-porosity phase change; Temperature- and surfactant-dependent surface tension; Robotic Pulsed GMAW (P-GMAW) validation across 25 layers.
key_params: Wire diameter: 1.2 mm; Nominal current: 125 A (effective 90 A); Voltage: 16–22 V; Travel speed: 0.17 m/min (2.83 mm/s); WFS: 4.7 m/min; Interpass cooling target: 100°C (flexible dwell time 100–180 s); Substrate: 8 mm steel; Layer height addition: ~1.8 mm/pass; Shielding: 99% Ar at 15 L/min; Droplet frequency: 60 Hz.
observations:
• Solves the multi-scale discrepancy between droplet impingement scale and large-scale 25-layer thin-wall geometry using a pragmatic FDM formulation.
• Surface tension gradient (dγ/dT) is identified as the single most critical driver of molten pool morphology and weld toe stability.
• In ER70S-6, sulfur acts as a surface-active element, altering Marangoni convection from outward to inward flow and producing deeper finger-like penetration.
• In ER316L, chromium and nickel contents dictate surface tension behavior, generating a broader and flatter molten puddle prone to lateral overflow.
• As layer stacking accumulates heat, molten puddle morphology shifts from a stable finger-type geometry to an unstable cylindrical pool with elevated weld toe surface tension pressure.
• Weld toe surface tension pressure exhibits abrupt spikes that reliably predict the onset of wall slumping and lateral sagging before experimental fabrication.
results:
• Captures the complete thermo-fluid dynamic evolution across 25 successive deposited layers with an average layer height build-up of 1.8 mm per pass.
• The model accurately pinpoints the critical layer threshold where lateral wall sagging initiates, matching experimental bead geometry within a 6.2% error margin.
• Molten pool central temperature drops rapidly as the arc passes, while weld toe cooling exhibits an intrinsic thermal lag driven by Marangoni circulating vortices.
• Surface tension pressure peaks at the weld toes exceed the capillary stabilization limit when local pool temperatures linger above 1350°C, triggering side slumping.
• Interpass dwell time management (100 to 180 s) successfully prevents cumulative heat buildup, maintaining the deposit start temperature at 100°C and stabilizing vertical wall growth.
future_work:
• Integrating real-time pyrometer and vision sensor data into the FDM boundary condition for adaptive closed-loop dwell time regulation.
• Expanding the 3D FDM fluid framework to multi-pass intersecting geometries and curved toolpaths prone to localized heat accumulation.
my_comments:
• Outstanding contribution demonstrating that FDM can simulate long-term multi-layer WAAM fluid flow without the prohibitive computational cost of traditional fine-mesh FEM.
• The use of weld toe surface tension pressure as a mathematical criterion for sagging provides actionable guidance for thermal path planning.

title: A Hybrid Ultrasonic Strategy for Super Duplex Stainless Steel Welding: Coupling Arc Induced Acoustics and Mechanical Vibration to Refine Grains and Balance Phases
process_methodology: Hybrid Ultrasonic TIG (HU-TIG) coupling ultrasonic-frequency pulsed arc (UFP-TIG) with mechanical ultrasonic rolling vibration (UV-TIG); In-situ high-speed imaging and infrared thermography; EBSD grain orientation mapping; Phase fraction quantification (γ/α balance); Uniaxial tensile testing and fracture morphology analysis.
key_params: Base metal: 2507 SDSS plate (250×150×3 mm); Autogenous TIG; TS = 200 mm/min; UFP current: peak current 230 A, base current 90 A, frequency 50 kHz, duty cycle 50%; UV parameters: frequency 20 kHz, amplitude ~15 μm, rolling distance 170 mm trailing behind arc; Shielding gas: 99.9% Ar at 15 L/min.
observations:
• Evaluates four discrete acoustic configurations: Conventional TIG (C-TIG), Ultrasonic-Frequency Pulsed TIG (UFP-TIG), Ultrasonic Vibration TIG (UV-TIG), and Hybrid Ultrasonic TIG (HU-TIG).
• High-frequency current pulsing (50 kHz) induces electromagnetic arc constriction, concentrating arc energy density and enhancing weld penetration.
• Arc-induced acoustic excitation raises melt pool peak temperature, which lowers melt dynamic viscosity and surface tension, substantially reducing acoustic attenuation.
• The pre-conditioned low-viscosity melt dramatically amplifies the penetration and cavitation efficiency of the trailing mechanical ultrasonic vibration.
• Intense acoustic cavitation and streaming break up dendritic skeletons and create abundant heterogeneous nucleation sites for intragranular austenite formation.
• Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) interphase boundary fraction decreases, reflecting a disruption of strict crystallographic orientation relationships during rapid solidification.
results:
• Electromagnetic arc constriction from 50 kHz current modulation deepens weld penetration by 32% compared to conventional unpulsed TIG arcs.
• Ferrite grain size is refined by 51%, reducing the mean grain diameter from 143.4 μm in conventional TIG down to 70.2 μm under hybrid ultrasonic processing.
• Austenite area fraction in the autogenous weld metal increases nearly threefold, rising from 6.9% to 20.0%, effectively restoring the critical γ/α phase balance without nitrogen gas additions.
• Kurdjumov-Sachs boundary fraction drops from 38.6% to 20.3%, replacing low-angle boundaries with high-angle interphase boundaries that resist crack propagation.
• Ultimate tensile strength rises from 732 MPa to 851 MPa (a 16% increase), while tensile elongation nearly doubles from 12.8% to 25.2% (a 97% improvement in plastic ductility).
future_work:
• Translating the hybrid ultrasonic strategy to multi-layer WAAM builds to assess phase stability under repeated thermal remelting cycles.
• Developing coupled acoustic-fluid-solidification phase-field models to simulate ultrasonic bubble collapse dynamics and δ -> γ solid-state phase transformation kinetics.
my_comments:
• Solves the longstanding dilemma of phase imbalance in autogenous duplex stainless steel welding without requiring costly active shielding gas mixtures.
• The synergy between arc-acoustic heating (reducing melt viscosity) and mechanical vibration (inducing cavitation) is a brilliant physics-based insight for WAAM melt pool control.

title: Achieving Fine-Grained Structure with Larger Ferrite Fraction via Local Dry Underwater WAAM to Enhance Corrosion Behavior of 308 L Stainless Steel
material: AISI 308L Stainless Steel (ER308LSi wire on SUS304 substrate)
process_methodology: Local Dry Underwater Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (LDU-WAAM) equipped with an argon gas drainage shroud creating a local dry working cavity; Comparative analysis against On-Land WAAM; EBSD grain boundary and KAM analysis; TEM interface segregation; XPS surface passive film analysis; Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
key_params: Wire: ER308LSi (1.2 mm); Substrate: SUS304 (200×100×10 mm); Deposition: 3 layers; Drainage gas: pure Ar at 45 L/min; Shielding gas: Ar at 18 L/min; Arc current: 140 A; Voltage: 19.5 V; Travel speed: 300 mm/min; Water depth: simulated marine environment; Layer height: ~2.4 mm.
observations:
• Local dry underwater chamber effectively isolates the arc and melt pool from surrounding water, maintaining a stable arc without water vapor contamination.
• High surrounding water heat dissipation dramatically increases the thermal gradient G and cooling rate R across all deposited layers.
• Rapid water cooling alters ferrite morphology from a conventional coarse skeletal network to a highly refined lath-like structure.
• The direct water contact on the exterior surface of the top layer induces an ultra-rapid quench, creating a dense equiaxed grain zone.
• Low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) and coincidence site lattice Σ3 boundaries proliferate due to thermal contraction stresses.
• Refined grain boundaries provide accelerated diffusion pathways for chromium atoms, promoting the formation of a dense, defect-free Cr2O3 and Fe2O3 passive film.
results:
• Rapid water extraction refines the austenite grain size from 42.5 μm in on-land builds down to 18.3 μm in LDU-WAAM middle layers and 11.2 μm in the top layer.
• Ferrite volume fraction increases from 7.4% (on-land) to 14.8% in the underwater middle layer and reaches 21.6% in the water-cooled top layer.
• Low-angle grain boundary proportion increases from 34.2% to 58.7%, significantly reducing interfacial dislocation pile-up and boundary energy.
• Pitting potential (E_pit) in 3.5 wt% NaCl shifts positively from 0.28 V_SCE (on-land) to 0.46 V_SCE (underwater middle) and 0.59 V_SCE (underwater top layer).
• Corrosion current density drops by more than an order of magnitude from 3.15×10^-6 A/cm² to 2.84×10^-7 A/cm², confirming substantially enhanced marine corrosion resistance.
future_work:
• Expanding LDU-WAAM to large-scale multi-pass structures (>20 layers) to evaluate residual stress distribution and hydrogen-assisted cracking susceptibility.
• Developing multi-phase thermo-fluid models incorporating localized water boiling and steam blanket heat transfer coefficients around the gas shroud.
my_comments:
• Proves that the steep cooling rates of underwater environments can be harnessed constructively to refine grains and boost corrosion resistance, turning an environmental challenge into a metallurgical advantage.
• The transition to lathy ferrite with Kurdjumov-Sachs orientation successfully prevents local Cr depletion along phase interfaces.

title: Phase-Field Modeling and Experimental Investigation for Rapid Solidification in Wire and Arc Additive Manufacturing
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology, 28:4585–4599
material: Al-5 wt% Si Binary Alloy (ER4043 wire on AA6061-T6 substrate)
process_methodology: Quantitative Phase-Field Modeling for non-equilibrium rapid solidification implemented in the in-house EasyPhase solver; Modified anti-trapping current j_at incorporating continuous growth (CG) solute trapping kinetics; Nonlinear thermal gradient model G(t) coupled with torch scanning velocity; Pulsed TIG WAAM deposition experiments; SEM, EDS, and EBSD microstructural validation.
key_params: Filler: ER4043 (1.2 mm); Current: 100 A; Voltage: 14 V; Travel speeds: 3, 5, 8 mm/s; Argon flow: 15 L/min; Grid resolution: Δx = 0.8 W0; Interface width: W0 = 10 nm; Capillary length: d0 = 1.05 nm; Liquidus slope: m = -6.6 K/wt%; Partition coefficient: ke = 0.13; Solute diffusion speed: VD = 10 m/s.
observations:
• Standard Karma thin-interface phase-field formulations assume local interfacial equilibrium, failing under rapid additive manufacturing cooling conditions (10^4 - 10^7 K/m).
• Incorporates the continuous growth solute trapping model into the phase-field anti-trapping current via a velocity-dependent partition coefficient k(Vp).
• Slower scanning speeds (3 mm/s) maintain high thermal gradients, promoting stable primary dendritic trunk growth along the build direction.
• Accelerating scanning speed to 8 mm/s flattens the temperature gradient, increasing constitutional undercooling and promoting secondary arm branching.
• Non-equilibrium solute trapping causes solute atoms to be engulfed into the solid phase, reducing solute accumulation in the mushy zone.
• Columnar dendrites exhibit strong <100> crystallographic texture, introducing mechanical anisotropy along the build height.
results:
• Successfully eliminates artificial interface-thickness-induced solute trapping while accurately capturing non-equilibrium partition kinetics during rapid WAAM solidification.
• Primary dendrite arm spacing (PDAS) decreases from 18.5 μm at 3 mm/s scanning speed down to 7.2 μm at 8 mm/s, matching experimental SEM observations within 8.5%.
• Solute concentration within the dendritic solid core increases from 0.85 wt% Si to 1.62 wt% Si as scanning speed rises from 3 to 8 mm/s, demonstrating solute trapping.
• Simulated inter-dendritic relative solute supersaturation (c/cl0) spans 1.21 to 2.33, closely aligning with experimental EDS point measurements showing 30.6 to 42.7 at% Si at grain boundaries.
• Grain morphology transitions from elongated columnar dendrites with aspect ratios >8 at low travel speeds to shorter, competitively growing dendrites at elevated travel speeds.
future_work:
• Coupling the non-equilibrium phase-field model with full 3D melt pool fluid dynamics to capture Marangoni convection-induced dendrite fragmentation.
• Extending the binary Al-Si phase-field formulation to multicomponent Al-Mg-Si-Cu alloys with multi-phase precipitation kinetics.
my_comments:
• A critically needed advancement in PFM: standard Karma anti-trapping currents break down at high interface speeds, and this paper provides the exact modified formulation needed for rapid WAAM modeling.
• Validating simulated inter-dendritic solute concentration against experimental EDS at grain boundaries sets a high benchmark for quantitative solidification modeling.

title: A Fast Simulation Method for Thermal Management in Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing Repair of a Thin-Walled Structure
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology, 132:1607–1619
material: S355 Structural Steel Plate and ER70S-6 Filler Wire
process_methodology: Subsea Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (SWAAM) in-situ repair; 3D laser scan point-cloud damage acquisition; Delaunay triangulation surface meshing and automated slicing; 2D explicit Finite Difference Method (FDM) thermal solver tailored for thin-walled geometry; Automated interpass dwell time optimization; K-type thermocouple and IR thermal camera verification against 3D Abaqus FE models.
key_params: Damaged plate thickness: 8 mm; 2D FDM grid: Δx = Δy = 2 mm; Time step: Δt = 0.005 s; Arc current: 115 A; Voltage: 14.5 V; Travel speed: 6 mm/s; Arc efficiency: η = 0.8; Convective heat transfer coefficient: h = 25 W/(m²·K); Maximum allowed interpass temperature: 150°C.
observations:
• Commercial 3D FEM codes are prohibitively slow for real-time robotic toolpath planning and thermal management during on-site repair.
• For thin-walled geometries, through-thickness temperature gradients decay rapidly beyond the immediate torch zone, justifying a 2D planar thermal simplification.
• Delaunay triangulation slices 3D damage point clouds into conformal deposition passes, generating raster infill paths and border perimeters automatically.
• Explicit finite difference formulation accounts for conductive heat exchange, convective surface losses, and moving arc heat input without requiring matrix inversion.
• Simulates dynamic interpass cooling breaks to keep the maximum local temperature strictly within the operational window (≤150°C).
• Two unexpected experimental arc ignition failures were seamlessly tracked by the thermal solver, validating model robustness under real-world process delays.
results:
• Achieves a 70-fold computation speedup compared to physical welding execution time using an unparallelized single-core CPU implementation.
• Thermal predictions match physical thermocouple measurements within ±10°C for all plate locations situated >15 mm from the torch center.
• Dynamic interpass dwell time scheduling successfully keeps pre-deposition temperatures within the 130–150°C window, preventing heat accumulation while reducing repair idle time by 34%.
• Compares favorably with 3D Abaqus FE simulations in far-field thermal distribution while completing in seconds rather than several hours.
• Successfully repaired an 8 mm dented steel plate across 3 stacked layers without encountering dimensional collapse or excessive heat-affected zone softening.
future_work:

title: Grain Refining by Ultrasonic Stirring of the Weld Pool
process_methodology: Direct ultrasonic probe stirring of arc weld pools using an immersed 0.5 mm tungsten rod encased in a 304 SS stiffener tube connected to a 3 kW, 20 kHz ultrasonic transducer; Investigation of probe offset distance behind the GTAW arc; Polarized light microscopy, SEM, EDS, and ASTM E112 grain sizing; T4 solution heat treatment to dissolve Mg17Al12 for precise grain boundary visualization.
key_params: Frequency: 20 kHz; Transducer power: 3 kW; Vibration amplitude: 14 to 28 μm (horizontal transverse oscillation); Arc current: 70 A; Arc voltage: 11.5 V; Travel speed: 4.23 to 6.35 mm/s; Probe immersion depth: ~1.5 mm; Probe offset distance behind arc: d = 2.0–7.5 mm; Argon shielding gas: 10 L/min.
observations:
• Directly introduces ultrasonic vibrations into the weld pool via an immersed tungsten probe, bypassing acoustic attenuation through the solid workpiece.
• Identifies three primary grain refinement mechanisms: cavitation-induced dendrite fragmentation, cavitation-enhanced heterogeneous nucleation, and grain detachment.
• Positioning the vibrating probe farther behind the arc (d ≥ 4 mm) significantly improves grain refinement compared to positioning it close to the arc.
• Nuclei and dendrite fragments generated near the arc center remelt due to intense superheat, whereas those formed in the cooler trailing pool survive and grow.
• Probe proximity to the solid-liquid mushy zone facilitates mechanical and hydraulic shockwave shattering of growing dendrite arms.
• Cavitation pressure pulses (200–1000 atm) induce local melting point elevation via the Clausius-Clapeyron equation (ΔTm = Tm ΔP ΔV / ΔH), increasing effective undercooling by 1.3 to 6.5 K.
results:
• In AZ31 Mg welds, ultrasonic probe stirring completely suppresses coarse columnar grains (width >150 μm), transforming the fusion zone into fine equiaxed grains averaging 43–52 μm.
• In AZ91 Mg welds, average equiaxed grain size drops from 71 μm in unassisted welds down to 32 μm with probe stirring, increasing the refined grain area fraction to over 85%.
• Refined grain area fraction increases monotonically with probe offset distance, expanding from 0% at d = 2.0 mm to 88% at d = 6.0 mm.
• Transverse oscillation amplitude increases from 14 to 28 μm expand the lateral width of the refined equiaxed zone across the entire weld bead cross-section.
• Enhanced grain refinement dramatically improves solidification cracking resistance in crack-sensitive magnesium alloys.
future_work:
• Extending immersed ultrasonic probe stirring to high-temperature refractory alloys and wire arc additive manufacturing of aluminum and titanium alloys.
• Direct synchrotron high-speed X-ray imaging of bubble nucleation and dendrite fragmentation around the vibrating probe tip in metallic melts.
my_comments:
• The landmark paper that established direct weld pool ultrasonic sonotrode stirring as a viable alternative to whole-part vibration.
• The survival-zone hypothesis (nuclei survive only in the cooler trailing pool) is fundamental to designing ultrasonic-assisted WAAM systems.

title: Research Progress and Application Scenarios of Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing: From Process Control to Performance Evaluation
material: Multi-Alloy Systems (Ti-6Al-4V, AA2319, AA5183, SS316L, Inconel 718, High-Entropy Alloys)
process_methodology: Comprehensive process and performance review across WAAM variants (GTAW, GMAW, CMT, PAW); Analysis of arc stability, droplet transfer modes, and heat dissipation dynamics; In-situ multi-sensor monitoring (vision, spectral, electrical, acoustic, and infrared thermography); Physics-informed machine learning and digital twin frameworks; Post-processing treatments (interpass rolling, ultrasonic impact peening, solution + aging heat treatment).
key_params: Deposition rates: GTAW (1–2 kg/h), GMAW (3–4 kg/h), CMT (2–3 kg/h), PAW (2–4 kg/h); Arc energy density: PAW > GTAW > GMAW > CMT; Heat input ranges: 0.2–1.5 kJ/mm; Interpass cooling temperatures: 50–150°C; Multi-sensor acquisition frequencies: 10–100 kHz for electrical signals, 30–1000 fps for visual/IR sensing.
observations:
• Systematically contrasts the thermal input, deposition rates, and droplet transfer stability of GMAW, GTAW, CMT, and PAW processes.
• CMT provides superior spatter-free deposition and lowest distortion, making it ideal for thin-walled aluminum and dissimilar joining.
• Identifies cumulative heat buildup as the root cause of bead widening, height humping, and columnar grain coarsening in tall structures.
• Multi-sensor fusion combining high-speed cameras, spectrometer emission, and electrical current/voltage waveforms enables real-time defect classification.
• Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) trained on thermal histories accurately predict bead geometry and solid-state phase fractions.
• Interpass mechanical treatments (cold rolling at 50–75 kN and ultrasonic impact peening) effectively close porosity, shatter columnar grains, and convert tensile residual stresses into deep compressive layers.
results:
• CMT reduces heat input by up to 35% compared to conventional pulsed GMAW, suppressing vapor loss of volatile elements such as Mg and Zn in light alloys.
• In-situ vision and spectral monitoring achieve defect identification accuracies exceeding 95% for porosities, humping, and lack-of-fusion flaws.
• Interpass cold rolling reduces peak tensile residual stresses by over 80% and frequently introduces surface compressive stresses exceeding -250 MPa.
• Post-deposition heat treatments restore isotropic mechanical properties in titanium and nickel alloys, elevating Ti-6Al-4V tensile ductility from 6% to >14%.
• Digital twin architectures integrating machine learning with fast thermal solvers reduce shop-floor parameter trial-and-error iterations by up to 60%.
future_work:
• Developing multi-physics digital twins with sub-millisecond edge computing feedback to regulate wire feed speed and torch motion dynamically.
• Standardizing qualification and non-destructive testing protocols specifically tailored for safety-critical WAAM aerospace and marine components.
my_comments:
• Exceptionally comprehensive state-of-the-art review that seamlessly links arc physics, sensing architectures, AI control, and metallurgy.
• Serves as an authoritative roadmap for thesis literature chapters on WAAM process control and hybrid manufacturing.

title: Comprehensive Analysis of the Properties of Stainless Steel 308L Tungsten Inert Gas Wire Arc Additive Manufactured
material: AISI 308L Austenitic Stainless Steel (ER308L wire on AISI 304 substrate)
process_methodology: CNC-controlled TIG-WAAM multi-layer thin-wall deposition; Vertical microstructural gradient profiling (OM, SEM, XRD); Microhardness mapping across bottom, middle, and top regions; Uniaxial tensile testing in longitudinal vs transverse orientations (ASTM E8); Electrochemical Tafel polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
key_params: Feedstock: ER308L (1.0 mm); Substrate: AISI 304 plate; Wall dimensions: 90 mm height, 7 mm thickness, 125 mm length; Current: 90–110 A; Voltage: 12–14 V; Travel speed: 100–150 mm/min; Argon shielding: 10–12 L/min; Interpass condition: natural air cooling.
observations:
• Fabricates a freestanding 90 mm tall multi-layer thin wall using cold-wire TIG-WAAM without interpass active cooling.
• Bottom layers exhibit fine dendritic austenite (γ) with skeletal δ-ferrite due to rapid heat extraction through the cold substrate.
• Progressive thermal accumulation causes a microstructural transition to coarse columnar and equiaxed dendrites in the upper build regions.
• Excessive interlayer heat buildup creates a visible collapse and spreading zone in the middle-to-upper layers where bead uniformity degrades.
• Microhardness exhibits a continuous descending gradient along the vertical build height, directly obeying the Hall-Petch grain size relationship.
• Tensile properties demonstrate significant anisotropy, with longitudinal specimens outperforming transverse specimens due to inter-track boundary orientations.
results:
• Microhardness decreases progressively along the build height from 242.5 HV in the fine-grained bottom layer to 180 HV in the middle, reaching 176.5 HV at the top layer.
• Tensile strength displays marked anisotropy: longitudinal specimens achieve an ultimate tensile strength of 547 MPa, yield strength of 364 MPa, and 35.5% elongation, while transverse specimens show 518 MPa UTS, 342 MPa YS, and 26.8% elongation.
• δ-ferrite morphology transitions from dense skeletal networks (ferrite number ~8.2) near the base to coarse vermicular and lath structures (ferrite number ~12.4) near the top.
• Tafel polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl reveals severe corrosion performance degradation along the build height, with corrosion rate escalating from 0.0048 mm/year at the bottom to 0.1112 mm/year at the top (a >23× acceleration).
• Pitting resistance correlates directly with microstructural refinement and low δ-ferrite content, with coarse top-layer dendrites exhibiting accelerated localized dissolution.
future_work:
• Implementing active interpass compressed-gas or thermoelectric cooling to suppress thermal accumulation and eliminate upper-layer collapse.
• Investigating post-deposition solution annealing (1050°C) to homogenize δ-ferrite distribution and eliminate vertical corrosion rate gradients.
my_comments:
• Provides rare, direct electrochemical evidence demonstrating that vertical thermal accumulation in WAAM directly degrades corrosion resistance by more than 23 times.
• Emphasizes the critical importance of active interpass thermal management for corrosion-resistant stainless steel additive manufacturing.

title: Enhancement of Heat Transfer Using Ultrasonic Waves: Experimental Investigation and Empirical Correlations
material: Pure Copper Cylindrical Probe and Distilled Water Subcooled Pool
process_methodology: High-frequency ultrasonic wave excitation (1.7 MHz transducer) submerged in a subcooled liquid bath; Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) non-intrusive laser flow visualization; Natural convection and subcooled nucleate boiling regimes under variable heat flux, water temperature, and transducer immersion distance; Empirical Nusselt number and heat transfer enhancement factor (EF) modeling.
key_params: Ultrasonic frequency: 1.7 MHz; Probe: copper cylinder (diameter 12 mm, length 70 mm); Heat flux range: q'' = 8,000 to 63,521 W/m²; Water temperature: Tw = 30°C, 40°C, 50°C; Subcooling degrees: ΔT_sub = 50°C, 60°C, 70°C; Transducer-to-surface height: H = 22, 35, 48, 65 mm; Rayleigh number: Ra = 4.2×10^7 to 1.6×10^8; Acoustic stream velocity: 0.1 to 0.3 m/s.
observations:
• Investigates the thermal-fluid coupling mechanism of high-frequency ultrasonic acoustic waves (1.7 MHz) on heat transfer enhancement in a liquid pool.
• High-speed PIV visualization reveals strong acoustic streaming jets emanating axially from the transducer face with velocities reaching 0.1 to 0.3 m/s.
• Acoustic streaming and cavitation disrupt the thermal boundary layer around the heated cylinder, converting stagnant natural convection into intense forced circulation.
• Imposing ultrasonic waves forces nucleate vapor bubbles to detach rapidly from the heated surface, suppressing the thermal insulation effect of stagnant vapor films.
• Raising bulk liquid temperature from 30°C to 50°C degrades the ultrasonic enhancement factor because lower liquid subcooling impairs acoustic bubble collapse intensity.
• Increasing transducer distance from 22 mm to 65 mm alters the acoustic radiation pressure field, with optimal standing wave resonance occurring at H = 65 mm under high heat flux.
results:
• Imposition of 1.7 MHz ultrasonic waves increases the average convective heat transfer coefficient by up to 133% compared to baseline unassisted natural convection.
• The maximum heat transfer enhancement factor of 2.7 (a 270% increase) is achieved at Tw = 30°C and low heat flux (8,000 W/m²), outperforming 40°C and 50°C pools by 35% and 86%, respectively.
• Elevating liquid bath temperature to 40°C and 50°C decreases the heat transfer coefficient by 17.2% and 46.8% due to dampened acoustic cavitation and reduced liquid density gradients.
• Optimizing transducer standoff distance to H = 65 mm under high heat flux (63,521 W/m²) yields a peak enhancement factor of 3.52, an 82% improvement over near-field placement (H = 22 mm).
• Newly developed empirical Nusselt number correlations (Nu = C1 · Ra^C2) predict the ultrasonic heat transfer enhancement factor within an average absolute deviation of ±3%.
future_work:
• Coupling 1.7 MHz high-frequency acoustic streaming models with liquid metal thermophysical properties (molten aluminum and steel) to predict boundary layer thinning in WAAM melt pools.
• Evaluating high-frequency acoustic cavitation thresholds under intense thermal gradients characteristic of directed energy deposition processes.
my_comments:
• Provides direct PIV velocity vector proof that ultrasonic streaming generates 0.1–0.3 m/s convective jets that thin thermal boundary layers and elevate heat dissipation by up to 3.52×.
• Fundamental reference for thermal-fluid modeling of ultrasonic-assisted additive manufacturing where accelerated cooling rates and boundary agitation govern grain refinement.

title: Novel Process Parameters Based Approach for Reducing Residual Stresses in WAAM
process_methodology: Thermomechanical Finite Element Analysis in Simufact Welding coupled with Taguchi L27 orthogonal array, Signal-to-Noise (S/N) ratio, and ANOVA; Moving Goldak double-ellipsoidal heat source; Quiet element method for progressive material deposition; Comparison of constant-parameter deposition versus a novel dynamic parameter gradation strategy along build length.
key_params: Wall dimensions: 11 layers, single-pass build; Current: 80, 100, 120 A; Voltage: 10, 15, 20 V; Travel speed: 70, 90, 110 mm/min; Goldak heat source parameters: semi-axes a = 4 mm, b = 3 mm, c1 = 4 mm, c2 = 8 mm, efficiency η = 0.8; Ambient temperature: 20°C; Layer-wise parameter variation: current held constant, voltage progressively increased, welding speed progressively decreased.
observations:
• Standard optimization approaches assume static, uniform process parameters throughout the entire build, which inevitably results in localized heat accumulation and stress peaks.
• ANOVA analysis reveals that arc current and voltage exert the dominant statistical influence on residual stress formation, while welding travel speed plays a secondary role.
• Attempting to reach global minimum residual stress by monotonically lowering current and voltage causes severe arc instability and bead discontinuity.
• Proposes a novel dynamic parameter gradation strategy that varies current, voltage, and speed along the length and height of the component.
• Increasing arc voltage while simultaneously decreasing travel speed under constant current produces the lowest effective von Mises residual stress profile.
• Dynamic parameter gradation alters the thermal cooling history, mitigating differential thermal contraction between early and late deposition tracks.
results:
• Static parameter optimization identifies local optima at 80 A, 10 V, and 70 mm/min, but leaves peak residual stresses excessively high due to uniform heat saturation.
• Dynamic parameter gradation strategy (increasing voltage, decreasing speed, constant current) lowers peak effective von Mises stress from 387.86 MPa down to 330.34 MPa on the baseline geometry (a 57.52 MPa reduction).
• Validation on an expanded complex build geometry demonstrates a major stress reduction from 1086.7 MPa (worst case) to 586.80 MPa (best case), achieving an average residual stress reduction of 173 to 210 MPa across the structure.
• Signal-to-noise ratio and ANOVA confirm that arc voltage and current account for over 78% of total variance in the induced thermal stress field.
• Controlled parametrical variation along the build length successfully stabilizes arc ignition without triggering bead humping or lack-of-fusion defects.
future_work:
• Implementation of real-time robotic closed-loop voltage and travel speed modulation driven by in-situ thermal pyrometer feedback.
• Experimental XRD and neutron diffraction residual stress measurement on multi-layer components fabricated using the dynamic parameter gradation schedule.
my_comments:
• Challenges the conventional paradigm of static parameter selection in WAAM by demonstrating that layer-wise parameter gradation can eliminate over 200 MPa of residual stress.
• Provides a practical, software-implementable parameter modulation strategy that does not require additional mechanical rolling or peening hardware.

title: Simulation of Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing to Find Out the Optimal Path Planning Strategy
process_methodology: Thermomechanical Finite Element simulation using Simufact Welding 6.0; Moving Goldak double-ellipsoidal volumetric heat source; Element birth-and-death technique; Comparative evaluation of five distinct deposition toolpath strategies: Raster, 2-Section Raster, Continuous Zigzag, Spiral (contour inward), and Zigzag + Spiral (contour offset); Longitudinal stress and 3D distortion vector analysis.
key_params: Goldak semi-axes: a = 4 mm, b = 3 mm, c1 = 4 mm, c2 = 8 mm; Heat source power: 1800 W (current ~100 A, voltage ~18 V, efficiency η = 0.8); Welding speed: 5 mm/s; Initial preheat: 20°C; Substrate: 16MnCr5 plate (100×100×10 mm); Deposition volume: 60×60×3 mm single buildup layer; Convective heat transfer coefficient: h = 20 W/(m²·K).
observations:
• Evaluates how five scanning toolpath strategies govern non-uniform cooling rates, transient thermal gradients, and residual distortion in a deposited layer.
• Distortion predominantly manifests along the longitudinal direction of deposited beads due to longitudinal thermal contraction strains.
• In raster patterns, each bead has two unconstrained ends exposed to outer edges, maximizing longitudinal shrinkage deflection and out-of-plane distortion.
• The 2-section raster strategy deposits adjacent passes before previous tracks cool sufficiently, creating steep lateral temperature gradients and the highest residual stress.
• The inward spiral strategy provides maximum inter-track cooling delay between concentric rings, ensuring uniform thermal contraction and minimal warpage.
• Enclosing zigzag infill within an outer perimeter spiral bead (contour offset) suppresses edge curling but slightly elevates central tensile stress.
results:
• Inward spiral deposition achieves the lowest out-of-plane distortion (0.24 mm) and minimal residual stress among all evaluated scanning patterns.
• The standard unidirectional raster strategy produces the maximum total distortion (0.78 mm), caused by unconstrained longitudinal shrinkage across open boundary edges.
• The 2-section raster strategy generates the highest peak effective residual stress (682 MPa) due to severe thermal asymmetry and inadequate inter-track cooling dwell time.
• Effective von Mises stress in the continuous spiral strategy is reduced by 28% compared to the 2-section raster pattern, accompanied by a 69% reduction in angular distortion.
• Simufact Welding simulations reveal that strategies minimizing edge-exposed longitudinal bead ends consistently exhibit superior dimensional stability.
future_work:
• Expanding the toolpath simulation from a single thick build layer to tall multi-layer thin-walled components (>20 layers) to assess cumulative vertical bending.
• Integrating thermo-elastoplastic constitutive models with solid-state phase transformation (austenite-to-martensite/bainite) kinetics for 16MnCr5 alloy steel.
my_comments:
• Clearly decouples the root causes of residual stress (non-uniform thermal cooling intervals) from distortion (unconstrained longitudinal edge exposure).
• Demonstrates that spiral deposition strategies are inherently superior for bulky block geometries, whereas raster paths require active mechanical edge clamping.

title: Influences of the Process Parameter and Thermal Cycles on the Quality of 308L Stainless Steel Walls Produced by Additive Manufacturing Utilizing an Arc Welding Source
material: AISI 308L Austenitic Stainless Steel (ER308LSi wire on SS400 substrate)
process_methodology: GMAW-based WAAM single-pass multi-layer thin-wall deposition; In-situ K-type thermocouple thermal cycle acquisition at layers L2, L10, L18; Optical microscopy and SEM metallography; Secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) quantification; WRC-1992 Schaeffler constitution diagram phase prediction; 3D optical profilometry surface waviness (Sa) analysis; Vickers microhardness (HV0.1) and uniaxial tensile testing (ASTM E8M).
key_params: Wire diameter: 1.2 mm; Current: 100 A; Voltage: 19 V; Wire feed speed: 3.2 m/min; Deposition travel speeds: 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 m/min; Linear heat input: 479 J/mm (at 0.2 m/min), 319 J/mm (at 0.3 m/min), 239 J/mm (at 0.4 m/min); Shielding gas: 98% Ar + 2% CO2 at 15 L/min; Wall geometry: 20 layers, ~40–60 mm height, 180 mm length; Interpass cooling target: 100–120°C.
observations:
• Investigates the combined influence of deposition travel speed (0.2 to 0.4 m/min) and repeated in-process thermal cycles on the geometrical and metallurgical quality of 308L stainless steel thin walls.
• Surface waviness (Sa) improves significantly as deposition speed increases because narrower, more stable melt pools restrict lateral molten metal sagging.
• Thermal cycles measured by thermocouples show rapid cooling in bottom layers (due to substrate heat sink), while upper layers exhibit cumulative heat retention and slower cooling rates.
• Microstructure consists of primary columnar/cellular austenite (γ) with residual skeletal/vermicular and lathy δ-ferrite situated along inter-dendritic boundaries.
• Solidification mode follows the ferritic-austenitic (FA) pathway, with the Cr_eq / Ni_eq ratio of 1.86 predicting 11–12% retained δ-ferrite on the WRC-1992 diagram.
• Secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) progressively coarsens along the build height from layer L2 to L18 as cumulative heat slows the local cooling rate.
results:
• Surface waviness (Sa) decreases from 286 μm at 0.2 m/min down to 138 μm at 0.4 m/min, representing a 51.7% enhancement in as-deposited surface smoothness.
• In the middle height region of the wall, secondary dendrite arm spacing decreases from 10.30 ± 1.38 μm at 0.2 m/min to 6.32 ± 0.97 μm at 0.4 m/min due to reduced linear heat input (239 vs 479 J/mm).
• Average microhardness increases from 153 ± 7.16 HV0.1 to 164 ± 8.96 HV0.1 as deposition speed rises from 0.2 to 0.4 m/min, driven by refined dendritic arm spacing.
• Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) improves from 483 ± 4.24 MPa to 518 ± 2.83 MPa and yield strength (YS) increases from 273 ± 3.51 MPa to 287 ± 2.12 MPa, meeting or exceeding wrought 308L standards (UTS ~515 MPa).
• Tensile ductility remains superior across all conditions, with fracture surfaces exhibiting dense dimples and elongation exceeding 45% (peaking at 52.4% for 0.2 m/min).
future_work:
• Developing closed-loop pyrometer-based wire feed and travel speed control algorithms to compensate dynamically for heat accumulation along tall thin-wall builds.
• Evaluating interpass active gas or cryogenic cooling to maintain fine SDAS and uniform hardness across builds exceeding 50 layers.
my_comments:
• Provides rigorous quantitative benchmarks for 308L WAAM linking linear heat input (239–479 J/mm) directly to cooling rates, SDAS (6.32–10.3 μm), and tensile response.
• The direct measurement of surface waviness reduction from 286 to 138 μm offers actionable data for minimizing post-process machining allowances.

title: Enhancement of Heat Transfer by Ultrasound: Review and Recent Advances
journal: International Journal of Chemical Engineering, Volume 2011, Article ID 670108, 17 pages
material: Multi-Phase Fluid-Thermal Systems (Liquid metals, subcooled liquids, water, molten alloys, metallic conduction media)
process_methodology: Systematic review and fundamental physical synthesis of ultrasonic wave propagation in thermal systems; Rigorous classification into power ultrasound (20–100 kHz, >10 W) vs high-frequency ultrasound (100 kHz–1 MHz); Deconstruction into primary physical mechanisms: Acoustic cavitation (transient implosive vs stable oscillatory), Acoustic streaming (Eckart bulk jetting, Schlichting boundary-layer shearing, Rayleigh vortex circulation), Acoustic radiation pressure, and thermal boundary-layer disruption; Synthesis across single-phase natural/forced convection, pool nucleate boiling, and solid-liquid phase changes.
key_params: Frequency regimes: power ultrasound (20–100 kHz) vs high-frequency (100 kHz–1.7 MHz); Acoustic power: 10 to 1000 W; Acoustic intensity: up to 10 kW/m²; Cavitation pressure threshold: negative pressure pulse overcoming liquid static pressure and cohesion; Acoustic streaming jet velocity: 0.05 to 0.5 m/s; Thermal boundary layer thickness reduction: up to 80%.
observations:
• Systematically classifies ultrasound applications into power ultrasound (20–100 kHz, >10 W, modifying the transmission medium via cavitation/streaming) and low-power diagnostic ultrasound (>1 MHz, <10 W).
• Identifies acoustic cavitation as the most violent physical driver: transient bubble collapse generates hydraulic shockwaves and localized micro-jets with pressures exceeding several hundred atmospheres.
• Deconstructs acoustic streaming into three distinct hydrodynamic regimes: bulk Eckart streaming (large-scale fluid jets), Schlichting streaming (micro-vortices within the viscous boundary layer), and Rayleigh streaming (circulating vortex cells).
• Demonstrates that ultrasonic agitation directly destroys the laminar thermal boundary layer near heated or solidifying interfaces, converting thick conductive resistance into turbulent convective mixing.
• In solid-liquid phase transformation, ultrasonic vibration accelerates melting/solidification rates and significantly narrows constitutional supercooling zones.
• Confirms that local acoustic sound pressure peaks and heat transfer enhancement factors are strictly in phase across fluid domains.
results:
• Establishes that power ultrasound (20–40 kHz) enhances convective heat transfer coefficients by 1.5 to 5 times (150% to 500%) across single-phase forced and natural convection systems.
• Thermal conduction in metallic solid media can be intensified between 2.25 and 5.55 times under resonant ultrasonic acoustic coupling.
• Acoustic cavitation micro-jets delay the onset of film boiling and elevate critical heat flux (CHF) in boiling and subcooled liquid pools by up to 400%.
• In solid-liquid phase change melting experiments, imposing 40 kHz power ultrasound reduced complete melting times from 275 minutes down to 72 minutes (a 73.8% time reduction).
• Identifies that ultrasonic enhancement is most pronounced in laminar flow regimes (low Reynolds number), where boundary layer thinning yields the highest relative reduction in thermal resistance.
future_work:
• Multi-physics numerical simulation coupling Helmholtz acoustic wave propagation with Navier-Stokes fluid dynamics and phase-change energy equations for high-temperature liquid metals.
• Investigating the synergy between ultrasonic acoustic streaming and Marangoni thermocapillary convection in micro-scale weld pools and additive manufacturing melts.
my_comments:
• The definitive fundamental review on ultrasonic thermal-fluid physics; provides the exact mathematical and physical mechanisms (Eckart, Schlichting, Rayleigh streaming + cavitation shockwaves) governing boundary layer thinning.
• Invaluable for formulating the ultrasonic energy source and convective heat transfer coefficients in phase-field and CFD models of ultrasonic-assisted WAAM.
